# Document: Runpod Python SDK

Source path: sdk/overview.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/overview.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/overview
Description: Use the runpod Python package to define GPU functions, deploy apps, call endpoints, build Serverless workers, and manage Runpod resources from one SDK.

# Runpod Python SDK

Use the runpod Python package to define GPU functions, deploy apps, call endpoints, build Serverless workers, and manage Runpod resources from one SDK.

The `runpod` Python package is the single SDK for building on Runpod. It includes the decorator-based app SDK that was previously shipped as Flash, the `rp` command-line interface, the client for calling existing Serverless endpoints, the Serverless worker SDK, and the API wrapper for managing Pods and other resources.

```python
import runpod

app = runpod.App("hello")

@app.queue(gpu="H100", dependencies=["torch"])
def hello():
    import torch
    return {"gpu": torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}

@runpod.local_entrypoint
def main():
    print(hello.remote())
```

Run the file with `rp flash dev main.py`. The `hello` function runs on a Runpod GPU, and `main` runs on your machine.

> **Note**
>
> Flash is now part of the Runpod SDK. If you have existing code that uses the `runpod-flash` package, it continues to work. To move an existing project, see [Migrating from Flash](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/migrate-from-flash).

## Get started

- [Quickstart](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/quickstart)

  Install the SDK and run a function on a GPU.
- [Migrating from Flash](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/migrate-from-flash)

  Move an existing Flash project to the Runpod SDK.
- [CLI reference](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/cli)

  Use the `rp` CLI to log in, develop, and deploy.

## Install

The SDK requires Python 3.10 to 3.14, and the features on this page require `runpod` 2.0 or later.

```bash
pip install runpod

# If using uv:
uv add runpod
```

If you already have `runpod` 1.x installed, upgrade with `pip install --upgrade runpod` (or `uv add 'runpod>=2'`).

Installing the package also installs the `rp` CLI. The same CLI is available under the longer name `runpod`.

## Authenticate

Log in once to store your credentials:

```bash
rp login
```

This opens your browser to approve access. After you approve, copy the API key the console shows and paste it at the prompt in your terminal. Credentials are saved to `~/.runpod/config.toml` and are shared by the SDK and the CLI. See [`rp login`](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/cli#rp-login) for other options, including named profiles.

> **Tip**
>
> You can also set the `RUNPOD_API_KEY` environment variable. This is the only environment variable the SDK reads for authentication.

## What's in the SDK

The `runpod` package covers four areas. Each one is independent, so you can use any of them on its own.

| Area              | Use it to                                                                                              | Main entry points                                               |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Apps              | Define functions and classes in Python that run on Runpod GPUs or CPUs, then deploy them as endpoints. | `runpod.App`, `@app.queue`, `@app.task`, `@app.api`, `rp flash` |
| Endpoint client   | Call a Serverless endpoint that already exists, by ID.                                                 | `runpod.Endpoint`                                               |
| Serverless worker | Write the handler that runs inside a custom Serverless worker container.                               | `runpod.serverless.start`                                       |
| API wrapper       | Create and manage Pods, endpoints, templates, and other resources.                                     | `runpod.create_pod`, `runpod.get_pods`, and related functions   |

## Apps

An app is a collection of Python functions and classes that run on Runpod. Create one with `runpod.App`, then attach resources to it with decorators. Each decorator defines a different kind of remote compute.

### Resource types

| Decorator    | What it creates                                                                     | Use it for                                              |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@app.queue` | An autoscaling, queue-based Serverless endpoint.                                    | Inference, batch jobs, and other request/response work. |
| `@app.task`  | One ephemeral Pod per call. The Pod provisions, runs to completion, and terminates. | Training, fine-tuning, and other long-running jobs.     |
| `@app.api`   | A load-balanced Serverless endpoint that serves a Python class over HTTP.           | Web services and APIs with multiple routes.             |

The following example defines one of each:

```python
import runpod
from runpod import App, Model, NetworkVolume, Secret

app = App("inference")

models = NetworkVolume("models", size=100)
llama = Model("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct")

# Autoscaling job queue on H100s, scales to zero when idle
@app.queue(
    gpu="H100",
    workers=(0, 3),
    dependencies=["vllm"],
    mounts={"/runpod-volume": models},
    model=llama,
    env={"HF_TOKEN": Secret("hf-token")},
)
def chat(prompt: str):
    import vllm

    llm = vllm.LLM(model=str(llama.path))
    return llm.generate(prompt)

# One ephemeral Pod per call
@app.task(gpu="H100", gpu_count=2, mounts={"/models": models})
def finetune(steps: int = 1000):
    ...
    return {"loss": 0.1}

# Load-balanced HTTP service
@app.api(cpu="cpu3c-1-2")
class Counter:
    @runpod.init
    def setup(self):
        self.count = 0

    @runpod.post("/bump")
    async def bump(self, body: dict):
        self.count += body.get("by", 1)
        return {"count": self.count}

    @runpod.get("/value")
    async def value(self):
        return {"count": self.count}
```

In this example:

- `chat` runs on an autoscaling queue endpoint with between 0 and 3 workers. Runpod stages the model weights on the host before the worker starts (`model=llama`), the network volume is mounted at `/runpod-volume`, and the `HF_TOKEN` environment variable is read from a Runpod secret.
- `finetune` provisions a two-GPU Pod for each call and terminates it when the function returns.
- `Counter` is served over HTTP. The method marked with `@runpod.init` runs once when each worker starts, and methods marked with `@runpod.get` and `@runpod.post` become routes. Workers keep state in memory between requests.

Specify hardware with `gpu=` or `cpu=`, which are mutually exclusive. For GPUs, use a short name such as `"4090"`, `"H100"`, or `"B200"`, a `runpod.GpuGroup` pool such as `runpod.GpuGroup.ANY`, or a `runpod.GpuType` device. Pass a list to allow several options. If you don't set `workers`, resources scale between 0 and 3 workers.

For every option, see [Resource parameters](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/parameters), [GPU types](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/gpu-types), and [CPU types](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/cpu-types).

### Call remote functions

Decorated functions keep their Python identity. You call them through methods that control where and how they run:

| Call                       | Behavior                                                                                 |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fn.remote(...)`           | Runs the function on Runpod and blocks until the result is ready.                        |
| `await fn.remote.aio(...)` | The async form of `.remote()`.                                                           |
| `fn.spawn(...)`            | Submits the work and returns a `Job` handle immediately, without waiting for the result. |
| `fn.stream(...)`           | Streams results back as the function produces them.                                      |
| `fn.local(...)`            | Runs the function in your local Python process. Remote storage isn't mounted.            |

For HTTP services defined with `@app.api`, call routes through the class, for example `Counter.post("/bump", {"by": 3})` or `Counter.get("/value")`.

`.remote()` and `job.wait()` don't impose an execution timeout by default. For streaming examples and how spawned tasks are cleaned up, see [Dev sessions](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/dev-sessions#call-styles).

### Local entrypoints

Mark the function that drives your app with `@runpod.local_entrypoint`. It runs on your machine and is the entry point for `rp flash dev`:

```python
@runpod.local_entrypoint
def main():
    print(chat.remote("Why is the sky blue?"))  # Blocks for the result
    job = finetune.spawn(steps=500)  # Returns a Job immediately
```

App discovery imports your modules synchronously. Keep blocking work inside an entrypoint or a remote function, not at the top level of a module.

### Storage

Attach storage with the `mounts` parameter, which maps a path on the worker to a volume:

- `NetworkVolume(name_or_id, size=50, datacenter=None, create=True)` references a [network volume](https://docs.runpod.io/storage/network-volumes) in a single datacenter. The app chooses a datacenter that works for every resource sharing the volume.
- `GlobalVolume(name_or_id, create=True)` references global storage that isn't tied to a datacenter.

Both types look up a volume by name or ID and create it if it doesn't exist. Set `create=False` to require an existing volume.

To choose between network and global volumes, see [Storage overview](https://docs.runpod.io/storage/overview).

#### Mount rules

Mount rules depend on the resource type:

- `@app.task` supports one network volume and one global volume, mounted at different paths that don't overlap.
- `@app.queue` and `@app.api` support one volume, mounted at `/runpod-volume`.
- Global volumes require GPU compute, for both tasks and endpoints.

Inside a remote function, `volume.path` returns the path where the volume is mounted. Read `.path` inside remote functions, not at the top level of a module. See [Storage](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/storage) for volume placement and billing.

### Develop and deploy

Use the `rp flash` commands to iterate on an app and ship it:

```bash
rp flash dev main.py  # Live dev session: edit, re-run, logs stream back
rp flash deploy       # Deploy production endpoints
```

A dev session creates temporary endpoints and deletes them when you press Ctrl-C. To learn more, see [Build an app](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/build-app), [Dev sessions](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/dev-sessions), and [Deploy an app](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/deploy). See the [CLI reference](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/cli) for all commands.

## Endpoint client

To call a Serverless endpoint that already exists, such as one you deployed from the console or with `rp flash deploy`, use `runpod.Endpoint` with the endpoint ID.

```python
import runpod

endpoint = runpod.Endpoint("ENDPOINT_ID")

# Wait for the result
result = endpoint.run_sync({"prompt": "Hello"})
print(result)

# Or submit a job and check on it later
run_request = endpoint.run({"prompt": "Hello"})
print(run_request.status())
print(run_request.output())
```

By default, the client uses the API key from `rp login`, `RUNPOD_API_KEY`, or `runpod.api_key`. To use a different key for one endpoint, pass it to the constructor: `runpod.Endpoint("ENDPOINT_ID", api_key="API_KEY")`. A key passed to the constructor takes precedence over the global key.

See [Send API requests](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/endpoints/send-requests) for more examples.

## Serverless worker

If you build your own worker container, use `runpod.serverless.start` to register the handler that processes jobs:

```python
import runpod

def handler(job):
    job_input = job["input"]
    return {"output": job_input}

runpod.serverless.start({"handler": handler})
```

To learn how to write handlers, including streaming, progress updates, and error handling, see [Handler functions](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/workers/handler-functions).

## API wrapper

The SDK includes functions for managing Runpod resources through the REST API:

```python
import runpod

pods = runpod.get_pods()
pod = runpod.create_pod("test", "runpod/stack", "NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090")
runpod.stop_pod(pod["id"])
runpod.terminate_pod(pod["id"])
```

## Limitations

- 5th-generation CPU instances (`cpu5c`) are only available in `EU-RO-1`. 3rd-generation instances are available in more data centers. See [CPU types](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/cpu-types#data-center-availability).
- Apps can scale workers quickly across several endpoints, so you may reach your account's worker limit. Contact [Runpod support](https://www.runpod.io/contact) to raise it.

## Next steps

- [Run your first function](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/quickstart) with the SDK quickstart.
- [Build an app](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/build-app) with several resource types.
- [Configure resources](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/parameters) such as GPUs, workers, and storage.
- [Migrate from Flash](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/migrate-from-flash) if you have an existing Flash project.
- [Learn about the runtime](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/runtime) that runs your code on workers.
- [Browse the examples](https://github.com/runpod/runpod-python/tree/main/examples/apps) in the runpod-python repository.


# Document: Get started with the Runpod SDK

Source path: sdk/quickstart.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/quickstart.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/quickstart
Description: Install the runpod Python package, log in with the rp CLI, and run your first function on a Runpod GPU in a few minutes, then deploy it as an endpoint.

# Get started with the Runpod SDK

Install the runpod Python package, log in with the rp CLI, and run your first function on a Runpod GPU in a few minutes, then deploy it as an endpoint.

This quickstart takes you from installing the Runpod SDK to running a function on a cloud GPU. You'll write a small app, run it in a live development session, and deploy it as a Serverless endpoint.

## Requirements

- A [Runpod account](https://docs.runpod.io/accounts-billing/manage-accounts) with a verified email address.
- [Python 3.10 to 3.14](https://www.python.org/downloads/).

## Step 1: Install the SDK

Create a project directory and a virtual environment, then install the `runpod` package:

```bash
mkdir hello-runpod && cd hello-runpod
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install runpod

# If using uv:
uv init && uv add runpod
```

Installing the package also installs the `rp` CLI.

> **Note**
>
> This quickstart requires `runpod` 2.0 or later. If you already have an older version installed, upgrade with `pip install --upgrade runpod` (or `uv add 'runpod>=2'`).

## Step 2: Log in

Authenticate with your Runpod account:

```bash
rp login

# If using uv:
uv run rp login
```

This opens your browser so you can approve access. After you approve, copy the API key the console shows and paste it at the prompt in your terminal. Your credentials are saved to `~/.runpod/config.toml`, and both the SDK and the CLI use them from then on.

> **Tip**
>
> To skip the browser, run `rp login --api-key API_KEY` with a key from the [API keys page](https://console.runpod.io/user/settings), or set the `RUNPOD_API_KEY` environment variable.

## Step 3: Write your app

Create a file called `main.py` with the following code:

```python
import runpod

app = runpod.App("quickstart")

@app.queue(gpu=runpod.GpuGroup.ANY, workers=(0, 3), dependencies=["torch"])
def matrix_multiply(size: int):
    # Import packages inside the function so they load on the worker
    import torch

    a = torch.rand(size, size, device="cuda")
    b = torch.rand(size, size, device="cuda")
    c = a @ b

    return {
        "size": size,
        "mean": c.mean().item(),
        "gpu": torch.cuda.get_device_name(0),
    }

@runpod.local_entrypoint
def main():
    result = matrix_multiply.remote(2000)
    print(f"Matrix size: {result['size']}x{result['size']}")
    print(f"Result mean: {result['mean']:.4f}")
    print(f"GPU used: {result['gpu']}")
```

This code does three things:

- `runpod.App("quickstart")` creates an app to hold your resources.
- `@app.queue(...)` turns `matrix_multiply` into an autoscaling queue endpoint that runs on any available GPU, scales between 0 and 3 workers, and installs `torch` on each worker. To request specific hardware, use a short name such as `gpu="4090"` or `gpu="H100"`.
- `@runpod.local_entrypoint` marks `main` as the code that runs on your machine. Calling `matrix_multiply.remote(2000)` sends the work to Runpod and waits for the result.

> **Warning**
>
> Import installed packages such as `torch` inside the remote function body, not at the top of the file. Top-level imports run on your machine, where the package may not be installed.

## Step 4: Run a live development session

Start a development session:

```bash
rp flash dev main.py
```

The CLI creates a temporary endpoint, runs `main`, and streams worker logs back to your terminal. The first run takes longer while Runpod provisions a worker and installs dependencies:

```text
Matrix size: 2000x2000
Result mean: 500.0412
GPU used: NVIDIA RTX A5000
```

Edit `main.py`, for example by changing `2000` to `4000`, and run it again. Later runs reuse the warm worker, so they return much faster.

When you're done, press Ctrl-C. The session waits for the running entrypoint to finish and then deletes the temporary endpoints.

## Step 5: Deploy your app

When your app works the way you want, deploy it:

```bash
rp flash deploy
```

This creates production endpoints that stay up after you close your terminal. List your deployed apps with:

```bash
rp flash app list
```

## Clean up

To delete the endpoints you deployed, run:

```bash
rp flash undeploy --app quickstart
```

## Next steps

- [Learn what's in the SDK](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/overview), including tasks, HTTP services, and storage.
- [Build a multi-resource app](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/build-app) step by step.
- [Configure resources](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/parameters) such as GPUs, workers, and storage.
- [Review the CLI commands](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/cli).
- [Call an existing endpoint](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/endpoints/send-requests) with `runpod.Endpoint`.


# Document: Resource parameters

Source path: sdk/configuration/parameters.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/configuration/parameters.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/parameters
Description: Reference for every resource parameter on @app.queue, @app.api, and @app.task in the Runpod SDK, including defaults and which decorators support each one.

# Resource parameters

Reference for every resource parameter on @app.queue, @app.api, and @app.task in the Runpod SDK, including defaults and which decorators support each one.

Every resource in a Runpod SDK app is configured through keyword arguments on its decorator: `@app.queue`, `@app.api`, or `@app.task`. This page lists each parameter, its default, and which decorators accept it.

> **Note**
>
> The parameters on this page require `runpod` 2.0 or later.

## Parameter overview

| Parameter              | Type                                    | Default                  | Queue | API | Task |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ----- | --- | ---- |
| `name`                 | `str`                                   | Function or class name   | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |
| `gpu`                  | `str`, `GpuGroup`, `GpuType`, or a list | Any GPU                  | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |
| `cpu`                  | `str` or a list                         | `None`                   | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |
| `gpu_count`            | `int`                                   | `1`                      | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |
| `workers`              | `int` or `(min, max)`                   | `(0, 3)`                 | Yes   | Yes | No   |
| `idle_timeout`         | `int` (seconds)                         | `60`                     | Yes   | Yes | No   |
| `dependencies`         | `list[str]`                             | `None`                   | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |
| `system_dependencies`  | `list[str]`                             | `None`                   | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |
| `mounts`               | `dict[str, Volume]`                     | `None`                   | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |
| `env`                  | `dict`                                  | `None`                   | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |
| `datacenter`           | `str` or a list                         | `None` (any)             | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |
| `image`                | `str`                                   | Runpod runtime image     | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |
| `registry_auth`        | `str`                                   | `None`                   | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |
| `model`                | `runpod.Model`                          | `None`                   | Yes   | Yes | No   |
| `max_concurrency`      | `int`                                   | `1`                      | Yes   | No  | No   |
| `execution_timeout_ms` | `int`                                   | `0` (no limit)           | Yes   | Yes | No   |
| `flashboot`            | `bool`                                  | `True`                   | Yes   | Yes | No   |
| `scaler_type`          | `str`                                   | Depends on resource type | Yes   | Yes | No   |
| `scaler_value`         | `int`                                   | `4`                      | Yes   | Yes | No   |
| `min_cuda_version`     | `str`                                   | `None`                   | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |
| `accelerate_downloads` | `bool`                                  | `True`                   | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |
| `container_disk_gb`    | `int`                                   | 30 (GPU), 10 (CPU)       | Yes   | Yes | Yes  |

The SDK validates parameters when the decorator runs, so a typo in a GPU name or an invalid worker range fails when you import the module, not when you deploy.

## Hardware

### gpu

The GPU or GPUs to run on. Accepts a short name such as `"4090"`, `"H100"`, or `"B200"`, a GPU pool such as `runpod.GpuGroup.ADA_24`, an exact device such as `runpod.GpuType.NVIDIA_H100_80GB_HBM3`, or a list of these.

```python
@app.queue(gpu="H100")
def infer(prompt: str): ...

@app.queue(gpu=["H100", "A100"])
def infer_with_fallback(prompt: str): ...
```

If you set neither `gpu` nor `cpu`, the resource can run on any GPU. See [GPU types](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/gpu-types) for every option and how each form is matched to hardware.

### cpu

A CPU instance type, such as `"cpu3c-1-2"`, or a list of them. `cpu` and `gpu` are mutually exclusive. See [CPU types](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/cpu-types).

```python
@app.queue(cpu="cpu3c-2-4")
def preprocess(data: dict): ...
```

### gpu\_count

The number of GPUs per worker, or per Pod for tasks. Must be 1 or higher.

```python
@app.task(gpu="H100", gpu_count=4)
def train(): ...
```

### min\_cuda\_version

The minimum CUDA version the host must support. Valid values are `"11.8"` and `"12.0"` through `"13.0"`. Setting it on a CPU resource raises an error.

```python
@app.queue(gpu="4090", min_cuda_version="12.8")
def infer(): ...
```

### container\_disk\_gb

The size of the worker's container disk in GB. Defaults to 30 GB for GPU resources and 10 GB for CPU resources. Increase it when your function writes large temporary files.

## Scaling

Scaling parameters apply to queue and API resources. Tasks don't scale: each call provisions one Pod.

### workers

The minimum and maximum number of workers. Pass a tuple `(min, max)`, or an integer to set only the maximum with a minimum of 0.

```python
@app.queue(gpu="4090", workers=5)        # Scales between 0 and 5
def a(): ...

@app.queue(gpu="4090", workers=(1, 10))  # Keeps 1 warm, scales to 10
def b(): ...
```

The default is `(0, 3)`, so resources scale to zero when idle.

### idle\_timeout

How many seconds a worker stays running after it finishes a request before it scales down. The default is 60.

### scaler\_type and scaler\_value

The autoscaling strategy and its threshold. `scaler_type` is `"QUEUE_DELAY"` or `"REQUEST_COUNT"`. Queue resources default to `QUEUE_DELAY`, and API resources default to `REQUEST_COUNT`. `scaler_value` defaults to 4. To learn how each strategy works, see [Endpoint settings](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/endpoints/endpoint-configurations).

### max\_concurrency

How many jobs a single queue worker processes at the same time. The default is 1. Raise it for I/O-bound functions that spend most of their time waiting.

### execution\_timeout\_ms

The maximum time a single job can run, in milliseconds. The default is 0, which means no limit.

### flashboot

Whether to use FlashBoot to reduce cold starts. Enabled by default.

## Code and dependencies

### dependencies and system\_dependencies

Python packages and system (apt) packages to install on the worker. Import Python packages inside the function body, not at the top of the file, so your local machine doesn't need them.

```python
@app.queue(
    gpu="4090",
    dependencies=["transformers", "pillow"],
    system_dependencies=["ffmpeg"],
)
def caption(image_url: str):
    from transformers import pipeline
    ...
```

When you deploy, the SDK also installs the packages listed in your project's `requirements.txt`. On the built-in GPU images, `torch`, `torchvision`, `torchaudio`, and `triton` are already installed, so they're left out of the build. See [Deploy an app](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/deploy#what-goes-into-a-build).

### accelerate\_downloads

Uses faster downloads for dependencies and model files. Enabled by default. Disable it if you run into compatibility issues.

### image and registry\_auth

By default, resources run on Runpod's runtime images, which already include Python and the SDK runtime. Use `image` to run on your own container image, and `registry_auth` to name saved credentials for a private registry:

```python
@app.queue(
    gpu="4090",
    image="ghcr.io/my-org/my-image:latest",
    registry_auth="my-ghcr",
)
def infer(): ...
```

Save registry credentials with `rp registry add`. See [Secrets and registries](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/cli#secrets-and-registries).

## Data and environment

### mounts

Maps paths on the worker to volumes. Queue and API resources support one volume at `/runpod-volume`. Tasks support one network volume and one global volume at different paths.

```python
models = runpod.NetworkVolume("models", size=100)

@app.queue(gpu="4090", mounts={"/runpod-volume": models})
def infer(): ...
```

See [Storage](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/storage).

### env

Environment variables for the worker. Values can be plain strings or `runpod.Secret` references, which the platform decrypts when the worker starts:

```python
@app.queue(
    gpu="4090",
    env={
        "LOG_LEVEL": "INFO",
        "HF_TOKEN": runpod.Secret("hf-token"),
    },
)
def infer(): ...
```

Create secrets with `rp secret add`. Secret values never pass through the SDK.

Runpod sets runtime identity and credential variables on deployed workers, so `rp flash deploy` fails if `env` uses a reserved name. Queue and API resources can't use these names:

- Credentials: `RUNPOD_API_KEY` and `RUNPOD_AI_API_KEY`.
- Worker identity: `RUNPOD_ENDPOINT_ID`, `RUNPOD_POD_ID`, `RUNPOD_BUILD_ID`, and `RUNPOD_RUNTIME_KIND`.
- App identity: `FLASH_APP_NAME`, `FLASH_ENVIRONMENT`, `FLASH_RESOURCE_NAME`, and `FLASH_BUILD_ARTIFACT_PATH`.
- Task and dev session internals: `RUNPOD_TASK_TOKEN`, `RUNPOD_TASK_PORT`, `RUNPOD_DEV_APP`, `RUNPOD_DEV_RESOURCE`, and `RUNPOD_DEV_SESSION`.

Tasks can't use any name that starts with `RUNPOD_` or `FLASH_`, in any letter case. They also can't use `PYTHONPATH`, `PYTHONHOME`, or `LD_PRELOAD`.

If your code needs its own Runpod API key, store it as a secret under a name that isn't reserved:

```python
@app.queue(cpu="cpu3c-1-2", env={"MY_RUNPOD_API_KEY": runpod.Secret("runpod-api-key")})
def manage(): ...
```

To call other resources in the same app, you don't need a key. See [Calls from deployed workers](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/deploy#calls-from-deployed-workers).

> **Warning**
>
> Values in a local `.env` file aren't sent to workers, and `.env` files are always left out of deployments. Pass every variable your workers need through `env`.

### model

A Hugging Face model that Runpod stages on the host before the worker starts, so cold starts don't download weights. Available on queue and API resources. Tasks download weights themselves.

```python
llama = runpod.Model("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct")

@app.queue(gpu="H100", model=llama, env={"HF_TOKEN": runpod.Secret("hf-token")})
def chat(prompt: str):
    import vllm

    llm = vllm.LLM(model=str(llama.path))
    return llm.generate(prompt)
```

Inside the worker, `llama.path` points to the staged weights. Libraries that use the standard Hugging Face cache, such as `transformers` and `vllm`, also find the weights automatically. Gated models need an `HF_TOKEN` on the same resource, from an account that has accepted the model's terms on its Hugging Face model page. A token from an account without access to the model still fails.

### datacenter

Restricts the resource to one or more data centers, such as `"US-KS-2"` or `["US-KS-2", "EU-RO-1"]`. Lowercase and underscores are accepted. By default, the resource can run in any data center.

Supported values: `US-CA-2`, `US-IL-1`, `US-KS-2`, `US-MO-1`, `US-MO-2`, `US-NC-2`, `US-NE-1`, `US-WA-1`, `EU-CZ-1`, `EU-RO-1`, and `EUR-NO-1`.

## Next steps

- [Choose GPUs](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/gpu-types) for your resources.
- [Attach storage](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/storage) with `mounts`.
- [Review recommended settings](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/best-practices) for production and development.


# Document: GPU types

Source path: sdk/configuration/gpu-types.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/configuration/gpu-types.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/gpu-types
Description: Choose GPUs for Runpod SDK resources with short names, GPU pools, or exact device types, and learn how the SDK matches each form to available hardware.

# GPU types

Choose GPUs for Runpod SDK resources with short names, GPU pools, or exact device types, and learn how the SDK matches each form to available hardware.

Set the `gpu` parameter on `@app.queue`, `@app.api`, or `@app.task` to choose the hardware a resource runs on. You can use a short name, a GPU pool, an exact device, or a list of these.

```python
import runpod
from runpod import GpuGroup, GpuType

app = runpod.App("gpu-demo")

@app.queue(gpu="4090")                          # Short name
def a(): ...

@app.queue(gpu=GpuGroup.AMPERE_80)              # Any GPU in a pool
def b(): ...

@app.queue(gpu=GpuType.NVIDIA_H100_80GB_HBM3)   # One exact device
def c(): ...

@app.queue(gpu=["H100", GpuGroup.AMPERE_80])    # Several options
def d(): ...
```

If you don't set `gpu` or `cpu`, the resource can run on any GPU.

## How GPU strings are matched

The SDK resolves a string in this order and raises an error listing the valid options if nothing matches:

1. `"any"`, which allows every GPU.
2. A pool ID such as `"ADA_24"` (case-insensitive).
3. An exact device name such as `"NVIDIA B200"`, or its enum name such as `"NVIDIA_B200"`.
4. A fragment of a device name, such as `"4090"`, `"B200"`, or `"h100"`. Every device whose name contains the fragment matches, so `"H100"` selects all three H100 variants.

Because strings are checked when the decorator runs, a typo fails when you import your module rather than at deploy time.

> **Note**
>
> Serverless endpoints (queue and API resources) select hardware by pool. If you pass an exact device, the endpoint uses that device's pool, so workers can run on any GPU in the same pool. Tasks run on Pods, which select by device.

## GPU pools

Use `runpod.GpuGroup` to request any GPU in a pool.

| `GpuGroup`      | GPUs                                                                                               |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ANY`           | Any available GPU                                                                                  |
| `ADA_24`        | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090                                                                            |
| `ADA_32_PRO`    | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090                                                                            |
| `ADA_48_PRO`    | NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation, NVIDIA L40, NVIDIA L40S                                            |
| `ADA_80_PRO`    | NVIDIA H100 PCIe, NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3, NVIDIA H100 NVL                                           |
| `AMPERE_16`     | NVIDIA RTX A4000, NVIDIA RTX A4500, NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada Generation, NVIDIA RTX 2000 Ada Generation |
| `AMPERE_24`     | NVIDIA RTX A5000, NVIDIA L4, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090                                               |
| `AMPERE_48`     | NVIDIA A40, NVIDIA RTX A6000                                                                       |
| `AMPERE_80`     | NVIDIA A100 80GB PCIe, NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB                                                       |
| `HOPPER_141`    | NVIDIA H200                                                                                        |
| `BLACKWELL_96`  | NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server, Workstation, and Max-Q editions                              |
| `BLACKWELL_180` | NVIDIA B200                                                                                        |

## Choose a GPU

- **For development**, use `GpuGroup.ANY` or a list of several pools so workers start quickly even when one GPU type is scarce.
- **For production**, pin a specific pool or device so performance and cost are predictable.
- **For multiple GPUs per worker**, combine `gpu` with `gpu_count`, for example `gpu="H100", gpu_count=4`.
- **For a minimum driver version**, set `min_cuda_version`, for example `min_cuda_version="12.8"`.

For pricing by GPU, see [Serverless pricing](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/pricing).
