# Document: CPU types

Source path: sdk/configuration/cpu-types.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/configuration/cpu-types.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/cpu-types
Description: Run Runpod SDK resources on CPU-only workers. Compare CPU instance types by vCPU and memory, and see which data centers stock each generation.

# CPU types

Run Runpod SDK resources on CPU-only workers. Compare CPU instance types by vCPU and memory, and see which data centers stock each generation.

Use CPU workers for work that doesn't need a GPU, such as preprocessing, routing, or lightweight APIs. Set the `cpu` parameter to an instance type ID:

```python
import runpod

app = runpod.App("cpu-demo")

@app.queue(cpu="cpu3c-2-4")
def preprocess(data: dict):
    ...

@app.api(cpu="cpu3c-1-2")
class Router:
    @runpod.get("/health")
    async def health(self):
        return {"status": "ok"}
```

`cpu` and `gpu` are mutually exclusive. To set fallbacks, pass a list, for example `cpu=["cpu3c-2-4", "cpu3g-2-8"]`. The `runpod.CpuInstanceType` enum lists the same IDs if you prefer constants, for example `runpod.CpuInstanceType.CPU3C_2_4`.

## Instance types

Instance IDs follow the pattern `cpu{generation}{type}-{vCPU}-{memory GB}`. The `c` types are compute-optimized and the `g` types are general purpose, with more memory per vCPU.

| ID           | vCPU | Memory | Type                       |
| ------------ | ---- | ------ | -------------------------- |
| `cpu3c-1-2`  | 1    | 2 GB   | 3rd gen, compute-optimized |
| `cpu3c-2-4`  | 2    | 4 GB   | 3rd gen, compute-optimized |
| `cpu3c-4-8`  | 4    | 8 GB   | 3rd gen, compute-optimized |
| `cpu3c-8-16` | 8    | 16 GB  | 3rd gen, compute-optimized |
| `cpu3g-1-4`  | 1    | 4 GB   | 3rd gen, general purpose   |
| `cpu3g-2-8`  | 2    | 8 GB   | 3rd gen, general purpose   |
| `cpu3g-4-16` | 4    | 16 GB  | 3rd gen, general purpose   |
| `cpu3g-8-32` | 8    | 32 GB  | 3rd gen, general purpose   |
| `cpu5c-1-2`  | 1    | 2 GB   | 5th gen, compute-optimized |
| `cpu5c-2-4`  | 2    | 4 GB   | 5th gen, compute-optimized |
| `cpu5c-4-8`  | 4    | 8 GB   | 5th gen, compute-optimized |
| `cpu5c-8-16` | 8    | 16 GB  | 5th gen, compute-optimized |

## Data center availability

CPU stock varies by generation:

- **3rd generation (`cpu3c`, `cpu3g`)**: `EU-CZ-1`, `EU-RO-1`, `US-CA-2`, `US-IL-1`, `US-KS-2`, `US-MO-1`, `US-MO-2`, `US-NC-2`, `US-NE-1`, and `US-WA-1`.
- **5th generation (`cpu5c`)**: `EU-RO-1` only.

If you pin a CPU resource to a data center with `datacenter`, choose one that stocks the instance type. If the resource shares a network volume with other resources, every resource must be able to run in the volume's data center.

## Limitations

- Global volumes require GPU compute, so CPU resources can only mount network volumes.
- `min_cuda_version` has no effect on CPU resources, and setting it raises an error.
- CPU workers get a 10 GB container disk by default. Change it with `container_disk_gb`.

## Next steps

- [Choose GPUs](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/gpu-types) for GPU workloads.
- [See every resource parameter](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/parameters).


# Document: Storage

Source path: sdk/configuration/storage.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/configuration/storage.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/storage
Description: Attach network volumes and global volumes to Runpod SDK resources with mounts, read volume paths in worker code, and avoid common storage mistakes.

# Storage

Attach network volumes and global volumes to Runpod SDK resources with mounts, read volume paths in worker code, and avoid common storage mistakes.

Use volumes to keep data that outlives a single worker, such as model weights, datasets, and checkpoints, and to share files between resources. The SDK supports two kinds of persistent volume:

- **`runpod.NetworkVolume`**: Storage in a single data center. Resources that mount it run in that data center. Works with GPU and CPU compute.
- **`runpod.GlobalVolume`**: Storage that isn't tied to a data center. Requires GPU compute.

To compare the two and decide which to use, see [Storage overview](https://docs.runpod.io/storage/overview).

## Attach a volume

Declare the volume once, then attach it to resources with `mounts`, which maps a path on the worker to a volume:

```python
import runpod

app = runpod.App("trainer")

checkpoints = runpod.NetworkVolume("checkpoints", size=10)

@app.task(gpu="4090", mounts={"/checkpoints": checkpoints})
def train(steps: int = 200):
    run_dir = checkpoints.path / "linear"
    run_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    # ... train and save to run_dir ...
    return {"checkpoint": "linear"}

@app.task(gpu="4090", mounts={"/checkpoints": checkpoints})
def evaluate(checkpoint: str):
    model_file = checkpoints.path / checkpoint / "model.pt"
    ...
```

Both tasks mount the same network volume, so `evaluate` can read the checkpoint that `train` wrote. The SDK places both tasks in the volume's data center.

## Volume references

Both volume types take a name or an ID:

```python
runpod.NetworkVolume(name_or_id, size=50, datacenter=None, create=True)
runpod.GlobalVolume(name_or_id, create=True)
```

- If no volume with that name or ID exists, the SDK creates it the first time it provisions a resource that mounts it. Set `create=False` to require an existing volume instead.
- `size` is the size in GB for a new network volume. Global volumes grow with your data, so they don't take a size.
- `datacenter` pins a new network volume to a data center. If you leave it unset, the SDK picks a data center that supports network storage and has hardware for every resource that shares the volume, respecting any `datacenter` setting on those resources. If you pin a data center that doesn't support network storage, provisioning fails before the volume is created.
- An existing volume keeps its ID and data center. Every resource that mounts it must be able to run in that data center.

## Mount rules

| Resource                    | Volumes                                  | Mount path                   |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `@app.queue` and `@app.api` | One volume                               | `/runpod-volume`             |
| `@app.task`                 | One network volume and one global volume | Any paths that don't overlap |

When you deploy an app, a task's mount paths also can't overlap paths that the runtime reserves: `/root/.runpod`, `/runpod-volume`, `/proc`, `/sys`, and `/dev`. A mount path overlaps when it equals a reserved path, contains one, or sits inside one.

Global volumes require GPU compute for both tasks and endpoints.

## Read the mount path in your code

Inside a remote function, `volume.path` returns the path where the volume is mounted on that worker:

```python
@app.queue(gpu="4090", mounts={"/runpod-volume": models})
def infer(prompt: str):
    weights = models.path / "llama" / "model.safetensors"
    ...
```

Keep these rules in mind:

- Read `.path` inside remote functions, not at the top level of a module. The SDK imports your modules locally to discover resources, and the volume isn't mounted there.
- Accessing `.path` raises an error if the volume isn't mounted on the current worker, or if it's mounted more than once.
- `fn.local()` runs your function on your machine without mounting remote storage.

## Cache model weights

To load a Hugging Face model without managing a volume yourself, use the `model` parameter instead. Runpod stages the weights on the host before the worker starts. See [`model`](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/parameters#model).

## Billing

> **Warning**
>
> Volumes keep incurring storage charges after you undeploy an app or delete a dev session. The SDK doesn't delete volumes for you. To delete a volume, see [Network volumes](https://docs.runpod.io/storage/network-volumes) or [Global volumes](https://docs.runpod.io/storage/globalvolume/overview).

## Next steps

- [Compare network and global volumes](https://docs.runpod.io/storage/overview).
- [Build an app](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/build-app) that shares checkpoints between tasks.


# Document: Configuration best practices

Source path: sdk/configuration/best-practices.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/configuration/best-practices.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/best-practices
Description: Recommended Runpod SDK resource settings for production, development, and cost control, including worker counts, idle timeouts, and GPU selection.

# Configuration best practices

Recommended Runpod SDK resource settings for production, development, and cost control, including worker counts, idle timeouts, and GPU selection.

These recommendations help you balance cost, cold-start latency, and reliability when you configure Runpod SDK resources. They apply to queue (`@app.queue`) and API (`@app.api`) resources. Tasks (`@app.task`) provision one Pod per call and don't scale.

## Production

- **Pin GPUs** to a specific pool or device instead of `GpuGroup.ANY`, so performance and cost are predictable.
- **Keep workers warm** for latency-sensitive work by setting a minimum of 1 or more.
- **Set `execution_timeout_ms`** so a stuck job can't run indefinitely.
- **Store secrets with `runpod.Secret`**, not as plain values in `env`.
- **Cache model weights** with `model` or a network volume, so workers don't download them on every cold start.

### Queue resources

Jobs can wait in the queue, so a small warm pool is usually enough:

```python
import runpod

app = runpod.App("batch")
weights = runpod.NetworkVolume("weights", size=100)

@app.queue(
    gpu=runpod.GpuType.NVIDIA_A100_80GB_PCIe,
    workers=(1, 10),
    idle_timeout=1200,            # 20 minutes
    execution_timeout_ms=600000,  # 10 minutes per job
    mounts={"/runpod-volume": weights},
    env={"HF_TOKEN": runpod.Secret("hf-token")},
)
def process_batch(items: list):
    ...
```

### API resources

HTTP clients expect an immediate response, so keep more workers ready and add a health route:

```python
@app.api(gpu="4090", workers=(3, 20), idle_timeout=1800)
class Inference:
    @runpod.init
    def setup(self):
        self.model = load_model()  # Runs once per worker

    @runpod.post("/generate")
    async def generate(self, body: dict):
        return {"output": self.model(body["prompt"])}

    @runpod.get("/health")
    async def health(self):
        return {"status": "ok"}
```

Load the model in the `@runpod.init` method so it's ready before the worker takes traffic.

## Development

- **Use `GpuGroup.ANY` or a list of GPUs** so workers start quickly.
- **Keep the maximum low**, for example `workers=(0, 2)`, to limit spend while testing.
- **Use a short `idle_timeout`**, such as 300 seconds, so workers scale down between runs.
- **Iterate with `rp flash dev`**, which deletes its temporary endpoints when you exit. See [Dev sessions](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/dev-sessions).

```python
@app.queue(gpu=runpod.GpuGroup.ANY, workers=(0, 2), idle_timeout=300)
def experiment(data: dict):
    ...
```

## Cost control

- **Scale to zero** with a minimum of 0 workers. The default, `(0, 3)`, already does this.
- **Use the smallest GPU that fits**, or a CPU instance when you don't need a GPU.
- **Shorten `idle_timeout`** for infrequent traffic.
- **Batch work** into fewer, larger jobs.
- **Delete volumes you no longer need.** Volumes keep billing after you undeploy an app.

## Trade-offs

| Workers          | Cost    | Cold starts                               | Best for                                    |
| ---------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `(0, n)`         | Lowest  | First request waits for a worker to start | Development, batch jobs, infrequent traffic |
| `(1, n)`         | Medium  | First request is served immediately       | Production queues, variable traffic         |
| `(3, n)` or more | Highest | Workers are always ready                  | Production APIs, high traffic               |

| GPU choice                                          | Cost        | Availability | Best for                              |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| `GpuGroup.ANY` or a list                            | Varies      | Highest      | Development                           |
| One pool, such as `GpuGroup.AMPERE_80`              | Predictable | Medium       | Production                            |
| One device, such as `GpuType.NVIDIA_H100_80GB_HBM3` | Predictable | Lower        | Workloads that need specific hardware |

## Checklist before deploying

- GPUs are pinned for production resources.
- Latency-sensitive resources have a minimum of at least 1 worker.
- `execution_timeout_ms` is set.
- Secrets use `runpod.Secret`, and every variable workers need is passed through `env`.
- Large models are cached with `model` or a volume.
- API resources have a health route.
- The app runs cleanly with `rp flash dev main.py --once`.

## Next steps

- [See every resource parameter](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/parameters).
- [Deploy your app](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/deploy).


# Document: Build an app

Source path: sdk/apps/build-app.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/apps/build-app.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/build-app
Description: Build a Runpod SDK app step by step: run a function on a GPU, add a load-balanced HTTP service, share data between tasks, and deploy it.

# Build an app

Build a Runpod SDK app step by step: run a function on a GPU, add a load-balanced HTTP service, share data between tasks, and deploy it.

This tutorial builds a small Runpod SDK app one resource at a time. You'll create a project, run a function on a GPU, add an HTTP service, stream results, share files between two tasks through a network volume, and deploy the app.

## What you'll learn

- How to scaffold a project with `rp flash init`.
- How to run queue functions on CPUs and GPUs with `@app.queue`.
- How to serve a stateful HTTP class with `@app.api`.
- How to stream results from a generator function.
- How to share data between tasks with a network volume.
- How to deploy the app with `rp flash deploy`.

## Requirements

- A [Runpod account](https://www.runpod.io/console/signup) with credits.
- Python 3.10 to 3.14 on your machine.
- The `runpod` package, version 2.0 or later. Install or upgrade it with `pip install --upgrade runpod`.
- Credentials saved with `rp login`. See [Authenticate](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/overview#authenticate).

## Step 1: Create a project

Scaffold a new project:

```bash
rp flash init my-app
cd my-app
```

This creates three files:

- `main.py`: An app with one queue function and a local entrypoint.
- `requirements.txt`: Packages your workers need. They're also installed locally for dev sessions.
- `.runpodignore`: Files to leave out of deployments. See [Ignore rules](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/deploy#ignore-rules).

Open `main.py`. It contains a complete app:

```python main.py
import runpod
from runpod import App

app = App("my-app")


@app.queue(cpu="cpu3c-1-2")
def hello(name: str):
    # this print streams back to your terminal during rp flash dev
    print(f"running in the cloud, greeting {name}")
    return f"hello {name}!"


@runpod.local_entrypoint
def main():
    # runs on your machine; hello() runs on a cloud worker
    print(hello.remote("world"))
```

`@app.queue` turns `hello` into a queue-based Serverless endpoint running on a small CPU worker. `main` is marked with `@runpod.local_entrypoint`, so it runs on your machine and calls `hello` remotely.

## Step 2: Run it in a dev session

Start a dev session:

```bash
rp flash dev main.py
```

The SDK creates a temporary endpoint for `hello`, runs `main`, and streams the worker's `print` output to your terminal. Leave the session running. Change the greeting in `hello`, save the file, and press Enter to re-run. Workers pick up the new code automatically.

Press Ctrl-C when you're done. The session deletes its temporary endpoints. To learn more, see [Dev sessions](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/dev-sessions).

## Step 3: Run a function on a GPU

Add a GPU function to `main.py`:

```python main.py
@app.queue(gpu="4090", dependencies=["numpy"])
def matmul_benchmark(size: int = 4096):
    import time

    import torch

    device = torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)
    a = torch.randn(size, size, device="cuda")
    b = torch.randn(size, size, device="cuda")

    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    start = time.time()
    for _ in range(10):
        _ = a @ b
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    elapsed = time.time() - start

    tflops = 10 * 2 * size**3 / elapsed / 1e12
    return {"device": device, "tflops": round(tflops, 1)}
```

Then call it from `main`:

```python main.py
@runpod.local_entrypoint
def main():
    print(hello.remote("world"))
    print(matmul_benchmark.remote())
```

A few things to notice:

- `gpu="4090"` requests an RTX 4090. See [GPU types](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/gpu-types) for other options.
- Packages are imported inside the function, so your machine doesn't need them. `torch` is already installed on the built-in GPU images, so it doesn't need to be listed in `dependencies`.

## Step 4: Add an HTTP service

Use `@app.api` to serve a class over HTTP. Mark routes with `@runpod.get` and `@runpod.post`, and setup code with `@runpod.init`:

```python main.py
@app.api(cpu="cpu3c-1-2")
class Counter:
    @runpod.init
    def setup(self):
        # runs once when a worker starts, before any request
        self.count = 0

    @runpod.post("/bump")
    async def bump(self, body: dict):
        self.count += body.get("by", 1)
        return {"count": self.count}

    @runpod.get("/value")
    async def value(self):
        return {"count": self.count}
```

Call the routes through the class:

```python main.py
@runpod.local_entrypoint
def main():
    print(Counter.post("/bump", {"by": 3}))  # {'count': 3}
    print(Counter.get("/value"))             # {'count': 3}
```

`Counter` runs on a load-balanced endpoint. Each worker keeps its own state in memory between requests.

## Step 5: Stream results

A generator function streams its output. Call `.stream()` to receive each chunk as the worker yields it:

```python main.py
@app.queue(cpu="cpu3c-1-2")
def tokens(prompt: str):
    import time

    for word in f"you said: {prompt}".split():
        time.sleep(0.2)
        yield word


@runpod.local_entrypoint
def main():
    for chunk in tokens.stream("hello streaming world"):
        print(chunk, end=" ", flush=True)
    print()
```

Calling `.remote()` on a generator returns every chunk at once. You can also call `.spawn()` and stream the job later with `job.stream()`.

## Step 6: Share data between tasks

Tasks run on a dedicated Pod that terminates when the function returns. To pass files between tasks, mount the same network volume on both:

```python main.py
checkpoints = runpod.NetworkVolume("checkpoints", size=10)


@app.task(gpu="4090", mounts={"/checkpoints": checkpoints})
def train(steps: int = 200):
    import torch
    import torch.nn as nn

    x = torch.randn(2048, 1, device="cuda")
    y = 3 * x + 1 + torch.randn_like(x) * 0.05

    model = nn.Linear(1, 1).to("cuda")
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.05)
    for _ in range(steps):
        loss = ((model(x) - y) ** 2).mean()
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()

    run_dir = checkpoints.path / "linear"
    run_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    torch.save(model.state_dict(), run_dir / "model.pt")
    return {"checkpoint": "linear", "final_loss": round(loss.item(), 5)}


@app.task(gpu="4090", mounts={"/checkpoints": checkpoints})
def evaluate(checkpoint: str):
    import torch
    import torch.nn as nn

    model = nn.Linear(1, 1)
    model.load_state_dict(torch.load(checkpoints.path / checkpoint / "model.pt"))
    return {"weight": round(model.weight.item(), 2), "bias": round(model.bias.item(), 2)}


@runpod.local_entrypoint
def main():
    out = train.remote()
    print("train finished:", out)
    print("evaluation:", evaluate.remote(out["checkpoint"]))
```

The volume is created the first time you use it, and both tasks are placed in its data center. `checkpoints.path` returns the mount path on each Pod. See [Storage](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/storage).

> **Warning**
>
> The network volume keeps incurring storage charges after the session ends. Delete it from the [Storage page](https://console.runpod.io/user/storage) in the console when you no longer need it.

## Step 7: Deploy the app

When the app works in a dev session, deploy it:

```bash
rp flash deploy
```

This builds your code and dependencies into an artifact and creates long-running endpoints in the app's `default` environment. To deploy to another environment, add `--env`, for example `rp flash deploy --env production`. See [Deploy an app](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/deploy).

To remove the deployed endpoints:

```bash
rp flash undeploy --app my-app
```

## Next steps

- [Learn how dev sessions work](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/dev-sessions).
- [Organize deployments with apps and environments](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/apps-and-environments).
- [Browse the examples](https://github.com/runpod/runpod-python/tree/main/examples/apps) in the runpod-python repository.


# Document: Dev sessions

Source path: sdk/apps/dev-sessions.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/apps/dev-sessions.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/dev-sessions
Description: Use rp flash dev to run a Runpod SDK app against temporary endpoints, stream worker logs, re-run on code changes, and clean up when you finish.

# Dev sessions

Use rp flash dev to run a Runpod SDK app against temporary endpoints, stream worker logs, re-run on code changes, and clean up when you finish.

A dev session runs your app against real Runpod hardware while you edit it. Start one with `rp flash dev`, pointing it at the file that defines your app:

```bash
rp flash dev main.py
```

## What happens in a session

1. The SDK imports your module and finds every `runpod.App` and its resources.
2. It creates a temporary endpoint for each queue and API resource. Tasks provision a Pod each time they're called.
3. It runs the function marked with `@runpod.local_entrypoint` on your machine. Calls such as `fn.remote()` go to the temporary endpoints.
4. Output that your remote functions `print` streams back to your terminal.
5. The session watches your project for file changes. When you save, it re-scans the app and refreshes the endpoints, so the next run uses your new code.
6. Press Enter to run the entrypoint again.

Press Ctrl-C to end the session. It waits for the running entrypoint to finish and then deletes the temporary endpoints. If cleanup fails, the command exits with an error and lists the endpoint IDs you need to delete yourself.

> **Note**
>
> Dev sessions don't run a local HTTP server. Your entrypoint calls remote functions directly, and you call `@app.api` routes through the class, for example `Counter.post("/bump", {"by": 3})`.

## Run once for scripts and CI

To run the entrypoint a single time, clean up, and exit, add `--once`:

```bash
rp flash dev main.py --once
```

The command exits with an error if the entrypoint fails, so you can use it as a smoke test in CI.

## Python version

In a dev session, and for task calls from your machine, the SDK sends your function's source code to the worker. The worker runs the same Python version as your machine so that syntax and language behavior match. Your local interpreter must be one of the supported versions: 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, or 3.14. An unsupported version fails with an error before anything is provisioned.

## Write code that works in a session

- **Keep blocking work out of module scope.** The SDK imports your module to discover resources. Put long-running code inside the entrypoint or a remote function. If discovery hangs on an import, interrupt it with Ctrl-C.
- **Import heavy packages inside functions.** Packages such as `torch` only need to exist on the worker.
- **Read volume paths inside remote functions.** Volumes aren't mounted on your machine. See [Storage](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/storage).
- **Guard local-only code** with `runpod.is_local()`, which returns `True` everywhere except inside a Runpod worker.

## Call styles

Inside an entrypoint, call your resources in whichever way suits the work:

| Call                       | Behavior                                              |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `fn.remote(...)`           | Runs on Runpod and blocks until the result is ready.  |
| `await fn.remote.aio(...)` | The async form of `.remote()`.                        |
| `fn.spawn(...)`            | Submits the work and returns a `Job` immediately.     |
| `fn.stream(...)`           | Yields results as a generator function produces them. |
| `fn.local(...)`            | Runs the function body on your machine.               |

`remote()` and `job.wait()` don't impose an execution timeout by default.

### Arguments and return values

Remote calls send arguments, return values, and stream chunks as JSON. Use JSON-compatible values: strings, numbers, booleans, `None`, lists, and dictionaries. The SDK converts values the way Python's `json` module does, including when a function calls another function on the same worker:

- Tuples arrive as lists.
- Dictionary keys that are numbers, booleans, or `None` arrive as strings.

Bytes, custom objects such as NumPy arrays or tensors, circular references, and `NaN` or infinite floats make the call fail with an error. Convert them before you pass or return them, for example with `tensor.tolist()`. For large binary data, such as model weights or images, write the data to a [volume](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/storage) and return its path.

`fn.local(...)` is a direct Python call, so it accepts and returns any Python value.

### Spawned tasks

Calling `.spawn()` on a task returns a job that owns its Pod:

- `await job.wait(timeout=...)` waits for the result, then tries to terminate the Pod, including when the wait times out or the task fails.
- `await job.cancel()` abandons the task and terminates its Pod.
- If you exit without waiting or cancelling, the task keeps running. Tasks can run indefinitely, so detached tasks keep billing until they finish.
- If the SDK can't delete a task's Pod, it prints a warning and keeps the ID in `job.pod_id`. Check the [Pods page](https://console.runpod.io/pods) and terminate it yourself.

## Costs

Temporary endpoints and task Pods bill like any other Serverless worker or Pod while they run. Dev sessions delete endpoints when you exit, but they don't delete volumes. See [Storage](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/storage#billing).

## Next steps

- [Deploy your app](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/deploy) when it works in a session.
- [See every rp flash dev option](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/cli#rp-flash-dev).


# Document: Apps and environments

Source path: sdk/apps/apps-and-environments.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/apps/apps-and-environments.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/apps-and-environments
Description: Learn how Runpod SDK apps and environments organize deployments, and manage them with the rp flash app and rp flash env commands.

# Apps and environments

Learn how Runpod SDK apps and environments organize deployments, and manage them with the rp flash app and rp flash env commands.

Deployments in the Runpod SDK are organized in two levels: **apps** and **environments**.

## Apps

An app is a named group of resources, declared in code with `runpod.App`:

```python
import runpod

app = runpod.App("inference")
```

Every resource you attach with `@app.queue`, `@app.api`, or `@app.task` belongs to that app. Resource names come from the function or class name unless you pass `name=`, and they must be unique within the app.

The app is registered on Runpod the first time you deploy it. A project can define more than one app; `rp flash deploy` deploys every app it finds.

## Environments

An environment is an isolated deployment of an app, such as `dev`, `staging`, or `production`. Each environment has its own endpoints and runs its own build, so deploying to `staging` doesn't affect `production`.

Every app has a `default` environment. To deploy somewhere else, pass `--env`:

```bash
rp flash deploy                    # Deploys to the default environment
rp flash deploy --env staging      # Deploys to staging
rp flash deploy --env production   # Deploys to production
```

You can also set an app's default environment in code with `runpod.App("inference", env="production")`.

### Common patterns

- **Single environment**: Deploy everything to `default`. Simple, with no separation between testing and production.
- **Multiple environments**: Deploy to `dev` while you work, `staging` for review, and `production` for users.

## Builds

Each deployment uploads a build: an artifact containing your code, its dependencies, and a manifest describing every resource. The environment then runs that build. Undeploying an environment removes its endpoints but keeps the app's build history. See [Deploy an app](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/deploy#what-goes-into-a-build).

## Manage apps

```bash
rp flash app list              # List your apps
rp flash app get APP_NAME      # Show an app's details
rp flash app delete APP_NAME   # Delete an app
```

Add `--yes` to `delete` to skip the confirmation prompt.

## Manage environments

```bash
rp flash env list                     # List environments
rp flash env get ENVIRONMENT_NAME     # Show an environment
rp flash env add ENVIRONMENT_NAME     # Create an environment
rp flash env delete ENVIRONMENT_NAME  # Delete an environment
```

These commands use the app defined in the current directory. If the directory has more than one app, or none, pass `--app APP_NAME`.

To remove an environment's endpoints:

```bash
rp flash undeploy --env staging
```

`undeploy` deletes the environment's endpoints and the environment itself. The app and its build history remain. If you leave out `--env`, it undeploys the `default` environment.

> **Warning**
>
> Deleting an app or environment can't be undone. Volumes aren't deleted and keep incurring storage charges. See [Storage](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/storage#billing).

## Next steps

- [Deploy an app](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/deploy).
- [See the full CLI reference](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/cli).


# Document: Deploy an app

Source path: sdk/apps/deploy.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/apps/deploy.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/deploy
Description: Deploy a Runpod SDK app with rp flash deploy: what goes into the build, ignore rules, size limits, Python versions, and how to call deployed resources.

# Deploy an app

Deploy a Runpod SDK app with rp flash deploy: what goes into the build, ignore rules, size limits, Python versions, and how to call deployed resources.

When your app works in a [dev session](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/dev-sessions), deploy it to create long-running endpoints:

```bash
rp flash deploy
```

The command finds every app in the current directory, builds an artifact for each one, uploads it, and creates or updates the endpoints in the target environment. When it finishes, it lists every resource in the app. Queue and API resources show a link to their endpoint. Tasks show as registered, because each task call provisions its own Pod.

To deploy a different directory, pass it as an argument: `rp flash deploy path/to/project`.

## Options

| Flag               | Description                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--env`, `-e`      | The environment to deploy to. Defaults to the app's environment, which is `default` unless you set `env=` on `runpod.App`.                                              |
| `--python-version` | The worker Python version used to pick dependency wheels: 3.10 to 3.14. Defaults to the Python running the CLI.                                                         |
| `--exclude`        | A comma-separated list of packages to leave out of the artifact, for example `--exclude scipy,pandas`. Excluded packages must already be installed in the worker image. |
| `--build-only`     | Builds the artifact without deploying it, and writes `APP_NAME-artifact.tar.gz` to the current directory. Use it to check what's included.                              |

## What goes into a build

Each build artifact contains:

- **Your project's source files**, filtered by the [ignore rules](#ignore-rules).
- **Your dependencies**, collected from the project's `requirements.txt` and every resource's `dependencies` list, and installed for Linux x86\_64 workers.
- **A manifest** describing every resource and its configuration.

You don't build container images. Resources run on Runpod's runtime images, which unpack the artifact and run your code.

On the built-in GPU images, `torch`, `torchvision`, `torchaudio`, and `triton` are already installed, so they're left out of the artifact automatically. If you use a custom `image`, every dependency is included unless you exclude it.

### Size limit

The artifact can be up to 1,500 MB. If it's larger, the build fails. To shrink it, exclude large packages that your worker image already provides with `--exclude`, or leave out project files with `.runpodignore`.

## Ignore rules

The SDK uses Git-style ignore patterns to decide which project files go into the artifact. It applies them in this order, with later rules taking precedence:

1. **Default exclusions** for virtual environments (`.venv/`, `venv/`, `env/`), caches (`__pycache__/`, `*.pyc`, `.pytest_cache/`, `.mypy_cache/`, `.ruff_cache/`), `node_modules/`, `.DS_Store`, `*.tar.gz` archives, and tests (`tests/`, `test/`, `test_*.py`, `*_test.py`).
2. **Your project's `.gitignore` files.** A `.gitignore` in a subdirectory overrides its parents for that subtree. Global and parent-directory Git ignores aren't read.
3. **A `.runpodignore` file** at the project root.

To include a file that an earlier rule excludes, add a negation pattern such as `!data/sample.csv`. If a parent directory is excluded, re-include the directory before its files. Symlinks are never included.

### Files that are always excluded

These paths are left out of every artifact, and negation patterns can't re-include them:

- `.env` files and variants such as `.env.local` and `prod.env`.
- Keys and certificates: `*.pem`, `*.key`, and SSH private keys such as `id_rsa` and `id_ed25519`.
- Credential directories and files: `.ssh`, `.aws`, `.azure`, `.kube`, `.docker/config.json`, `.netrc`, `.npmrc`, `.pypirc`, `.git-credentials`, `.boto`, and `service-account*.json`.
- Internal paths: `.git`, `.runpod`, `.flash`, and the root `env/` directory.

> **Warning**
>
> These safeguards match file names. They don't scan file contents for secrets. Review a `--build-only` artifact before deploying, and pass credentials to workers with `env` and `runpod.Secret`.

## Call deployed resources

From another codebase, use `runpod.Queue`, `runpod.Api`, and `runpod.Task` to call resources in a deployed app by name:

```python
import runpod

transcribe = runpod.Queue(app="media", name="transcribe")
result = transcribe.remote(audio_url="https://example.com/audio.mp3")

inference = runpod.Api(app="media", name="inference")
response = inference.post("/generate", {"prompt": "hi"})

train = runpod.Task(app="media", name="train")
job = train.spawn(steps=500)  # Use train.remote(...) to wait for the result
```

Each stub targets the `default` environment unless you pass `env=`. Arguments and results must be JSON-compatible. See [Arguments and return values](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/dev-sessions#arguments-and-return-values).

From your machine, these calls use your account credentials from `rp login` or `RUNPOD_API_KEY`, so they can reach any app that your API key has permission to call.

### Calls from deployed workers

Deployed workers don't receive your API key. Runpod issues each endpoint and task Pod its own runtime credentials, and the SDK uses them for calls the worker makes to other resources. With these credentials, a deployed worker can call only resources in its own app and environment. This applies to `.remote()` calls on your resources and to `runpod.Queue`, `runpod.Api`, and `runpod.Task` stubs. A call to another app or environment fails.

Because Runpod sets these credentials, your resources can't use some environment variable names. See [env](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/parameters#env).

You can also call a deployed queue endpoint by ID with the [endpoint client](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/overview#endpoint-client), or send HTTP requests to it directly. See [Send API requests](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/endpoints/send-requests).

## Update and remove a deployment

To deploy new code, run `rp flash deploy` again with the same environment. To remove an environment's endpoints, run:

```bash
rp flash undeploy --env ENVIRONMENT_NAME
```

See [Apps and environments](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/apps-and-environments).

## Next steps

- [Organize deployments with environments](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/apps-and-environments).
- [See every rp flash deploy option](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/cli#rp-flash-deploy).


# Document: rp CLI reference

Source path: sdk/cli.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/cli.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/cli
Description: Reference for the rp CLI that ships with the runpod Python package: log in, scaffold apps, run live dev sessions, deploy, and manage SSH keys and Pods.

# rp CLI reference

Reference for the rp CLI that ships with the runpod Python package: log in, scaffold apps, run live dev sessions, deploy, and manage SSH keys and Pods.

The `rp` CLI is installed with the `runpod` Python package. Use it to authenticate, develop and deploy apps, and work with Pods and SSH keys. The same CLI is also available under the name `runpod`, so `rp flash deploy` and `runpod flash deploy` are equivalent.

> **Note**
>
> The `rp` CLI is separate from [`runpodctl`](https://docs.runpod.io/runpodctl/overview), which is a standalone binary with a different set of commands.

## Command summary

```bash
# Auth
rp login

# Apps
rp flash init my-app
rp flash dev main.py
rp flash deploy
rp flash app list
rp flash env list --app my-app
rp flash undeploy --app my-app

# Secrets and registries
rp secret add SECRET_NAME
rp registry add REGISTRY_NAME

# Logs and updates
rp logs POD_ID --follow
rp update

# SSH
rp ssh add
rp ssh list
rp ssh POD_ID

# Pods
rp pod list
rp pod create
rp pod connect POD_ID
```

App lifecycle commands live under `rp flash`. Login, secrets, registries, logs, updates, SSH, and Pod commands live at the root. Run `rp --help` or `rp COMMAND --help` for details on any command.

## rp login

Authenticate with Runpod and save your credentials to `~/.runpod/config.toml`:

```bash
rp login                       # Approve in your browser, then paste the key
rp login --api-key API_KEY     # Store a key directly
rp login --profile staging     # Save credentials to a named profile
```

Without `--api-key` or `--agent`, `rp login` opens the Runpod console so you can approve the login request. After you approve, the console shows a new API key. Copy it and paste it at the prompt in your terminal. The input is hidden, and the CLI verifies the key before saving it. If the key is empty or rejected, you can try again up to three times before you need to run `rp login` again.

Browser login needs an interactive terminal to read the pasted key. In CI pipelines or scripts, set the `RUNPOD_API_KEY` environment variable or run `rp login --api-key API_KEY` instead. When an AI coding agent runs the login for you, use [agent login](#log-in-with-an-emailed-code).

Use `--profile PROFILE_NAME` with either login method to update only that profile. The default profile is `default`. To print the approval URL instead of opening a browser, add `--no-open`.

### Log in with an emailed code

When an AI coding agent or a script runs `rp login` for you, it can't approve access in a browser or answer an interactive prompt. Agent login replaces both with a verification code sent to your email, split across two commands. First, request the code:

```bash
rp login --agent --email EMAIL_ADDRESS
```

The command sends a six-digit code to that address and exits, printing the command that completes the login. Once you have the code, run:

```bash
rp login --agent --code CODE
```

This exchanges the code for an API key and saves it to `~/.runpod/config.toml`. Until then, the pending login is stored in `~/.runpod` with owner-only permissions, and it's deleted after your credentials are saved. Pass the same `--profile` to both commands because each profile keeps its own pending login.

If the code is rejected, run the second command again with the correct code. If the CLI reports that the login attempt expired or is no longer valid, request a new code with `--email`. Treat the code as a secret: command arguments can appear in shell history and process listings.

## rp flash init

Scaffold a new app project:

```bash
rp flash init my-app   # Create a project in a new my-app directory
rp flash init .        # Create a project in the current directory
```

This writes `main.py` (an app with one queue function and a local entrypoint), `requirements.txt`, and `.runpodignore`. Existing files aren't overwritten unless you add `--force`. See [Build an app](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/build-app).

## rp flash dev

Run a live development session for the app defined in a file:

```bash
rp flash dev main.py
```

The session creates temporary endpoints, runs the function marked with `@runpod.local_entrypoint`, and streams worker logs back to your terminal. Edit your code, then press Enter to re-run. Workers pick up the new code automatically.

See [Dev sessions](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/dev-sessions) for how sessions work. To run the entrypoint once and exit, which is useful for scripts and CI, add `--once`:

```bash
rp flash dev main.py --once
```

When you press Ctrl-C, the session waits for the running entrypoint to finish and then deletes its endpoints. If cleanup fails, the command exits with an error and lists the endpoint IDs you need to delete.

> **Tip**
>
> App discovery imports your modules synchronously. Keep blocking work inside an entrypoint or a remote function. If discovery hangs on an import, interrupt it with Ctrl-C.

## rp flash deploy

Build and deploy the app in the current project:

```bash
rp flash deploy
```

This packages and deploys every app found in the current directory. To deploy another directory, pass its path, for example `rp flash deploy path/to/project`. Flags:

| Flag                       | Description                                                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--env`, `-e`              | Deploy to a specific environment. Defaults to the app's environment, which is `default` unless set in code.                                    |
| `--exclude PACKAGES`       | Leave a comma-separated list of packages out of the artifact, for example `--exclude scipy,pandas`. They must then come from the worker image. |
| `--python-version VERSION` | The worker Python version used to pick dependency wheels, from 3.10 to 3.14. Defaults to the Python running the CLI.                           |
| `--build-only`             | Build the artifact without deploying it, and write `APP_NAME-artifact.tar.gz` to the current directory. This replaces `flash build`.           |

To learn what goes into the artifact, including ignore rules and the size limit, see [Deploy an app](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/deploy).

## rp flash app

Manage the apps you've deployed:

```bash
rp flash app list              # List your apps
rp flash app get APP_NAME      # Show an app's details
rp flash app delete APP_NAME   # Delete an app (add --yes to skip the prompt)
```

## rp flash env

Manage an app's environments, such as `dev`, `staging`, and `production`:

```bash
rp flash env list --app my-app       # List environments
rp flash env get ENVIRONMENT_NAME    # Show an environment's endpoints and status
rp flash env add ENVIRONMENT_NAME    # Create an environment
rp flash env delete ENVIRONMENT_NAME # Delete an environment
```

The `env` commands use the app in the current directory. If the directory has no app or more than one, pass `--app APP_NAME`.

## rp flash undeploy

Delete an environment's endpoints and the environment itself:

```bash
rp flash undeploy --app my-app              # Undeploy the default environment
rp flash undeploy --app my-app --env staging
```

The app and its build history remain. `--app` is optional when the current directory has one app. Add `--yes` to skip the confirmation prompt.

> **Warning**
>
> Undeploying an app doesn't delete network volumes it created. Volumes continue to incur storage charges until you delete them. See [Network volumes](https://docs.runpod.io/storage/network-volumes) to learn how to delete a volume.

## Secrets and registries

Store secrets that your app reads with `runpod.Secret`, and save credentials for private container registries:

```bash
rp secret add SECRET_NAME       # Create a secret (prompts for the value)
rp secret list                  # List secrets
rp secret delete SECRET_NAME    # Delete a secret

rp registry add REGISTRY_NAME   # Save registry credentials (prompts for username and password)
rp registry list                # List saved credentials
rp registry delete REGISTRY_NAME
```

`rp secret add` also accepts `--value` and `--description`, and `rp registry add` accepts `--username` and `--password`. If you leave them out, the CLI prompts for them, which keeps the values out of your shell history. Reference a secret in code with `env={"HF_TOKEN": runpod.Secret("SECRET_NAME")}`, and registry credentials with `registry_auth="REGISTRY_NAME"`.

## rp logs

Show a Pod's container and system logs, such as a Pod started by `@app.task`:

```bash
rp logs POD_ID                    # Show recent logs
rp logs POD_ID --follow           # Stream new logs as they arrive
rp logs POD_ID --tail 500         # Backfill the last 500 lines (default 100)
rp logs POD_ID --type container   # Only container logs (all, container, or system)
```

## rp update

Update the `runpod` package, which includes the CLI, to the latest version:

```bash
rp update
rp update --version 2.0.0   # Install a specific version
```

## rp ssh

Manage SSH keys on your account and connect to Pods:

```bash
rp ssh add       # Add a key to your account
rp ssh list      # List the keys on your account
rp ssh POD_ID    # Open a terminal on a Pod
```

`rp ssh add` generates a new key if you don't pass one. To use an existing key, pass `--key` or `--key-file`. Keys are stored in `~/.runpod/ssh/`.

## rp pod

Work with Pods:

```bash
rp pod list
rp pod create
rp pod connect POD_ID    # Same as rp ssh POD_ID
```

## Next steps

- [Get started with the SDK](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/quickstart).
- [See how Flash CLI commands map to rp](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/migrate-from-flash#step-2-update-your-cli-commands).


# Document: Runpod SDK runtime

Source path: sdk/runtime.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/runtime.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/runtime
Description: Learn what the runpod-sdk-runtime package does, where its source lives, and when you need to think about it separately from the runpod Python SDK.

# Runpod SDK runtime

Learn what the runpod-sdk-runtime package does, where its source lives, and when you need to think about it separately from the runpod Python SDK.

When you run an app built with the Runpod SDK, two pieces of code are involved:

- **The SDK** (`runpod`) runs on your machine. It defines your app, talks to the Runpod API, and powers the `rp` CLI.
- **The runtime** (`runpod-sdk-runtime`) runs on each worker. It loads your code, binds storage and other resources, and executes your functions when requests arrive.

The runtime used to ship inside the SDK. It now lives in its own repository, [runpod-workers/sdk-runtime](https://github.com/runpod-workers/sdk-runtime), and is released as a separate package. This lets Runpod ship runtime fixes and update worker images without requiring you to upgrade the SDK, and the reverse.

## How the runtime gets onto workers

You don't install the runtime yourself. Runpod handles it in one of two ways, depending on how your resource is configured:

- **Default images.** Runpod's worker images come with the runtime already installed and cached on Runpod machines, so workers start without an extra install step.
- **Custom images.** If you set `image=` on a resource, the worker installs `runpod-sdk-runtime` when it starts. Your image needs Python and `pip`, and the worker needs network access to the package index.

## When you need the runtime separately

Most users never interact with the runtime directly. You might need to think about it in these cases:

- **You use a custom container image.** The image must be able to install `runpod-sdk-runtime` at startup. If the install fails, the worker can't start and requests time out.
- **You need a specific runtime version.** For example, to pick up a fix before it reaches the default images, or to pin a known-good version.
- **You're debugging worker startup.** Worker logs that mention the runtime or its bootstrap step come from this package, not from your code or the SDK.
- **You want to read or contribute to the worker-side code.** It lives in the [runpod-workers/sdk-runtime](https://github.com/runpod-workers/sdk-runtime) repository, not in runpod-python.

## Serverless workers you build yourself

The runtime is only used by apps defined with `runpod.App`. If you build your own worker container with a handler function and `runpod.serverless.start`, you don't need the runtime. Keep installing the `runpod` package in your image as before. See [Handler functions](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/workers/handler-functions).

## Next steps

- [Read the SDK overview](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/overview).
- [Migrate from Flash](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/migrate-from-flash) if you have an existing Flash project.


# Document: Migrate from Flash to the Runpod SDK

Source path: sdk/migrate-from-flash.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/sdk/migrate-from-flash.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/migrate-from-flash
Description: Move an existing Flash project to the unified Runpod SDK: install runpod, update CLI commands and code, check behavior changes, and test before redeploying.

# Migrate from Flash to the Runpod SDK

Move an existing Flash project to the unified Runpod SDK: install runpod, update CLI commands and code, check behavior changes, and test before redeploying.

Flash is now part of the `runpod` Python package, so there's one SDK, one package to install, and one CLI. This guide shows where each part of Flash lives in the Runpod SDK and walks you through moving an existing Flash project over.

> **Note**
>
> **`runpod-flash` is deprecated.** Your existing Flash code and deployed endpoints keep working, but after the deprecation date listed on the [Flash overview](https://docs.runpod.io/flash/overview), the package gets no fixes or updates. New features land only in the `runpod` package. For details, see the [deprecation timeline](#flash-deprecation-timeline).

## What changed at a glance

- **One package.** Install `runpod` instead of `runpod-flash`. The app SDK, the endpoint client, the Serverless worker SDK, and the API wrapper all ship together.
- **One CLI.** Flash commands now run as `rp flash COMMAND`. Account commands such as `rp login` live at the root of the same CLI. The CLI is also available as `runpod`, so `runpod flash deploy` works too.
- **One login.** `rp login` saves credentials to `~/.runpod/config.toml`, which the whole SDK reads. `RUNPOD_API_KEY` is the only environment variable for authentication.
- **An app-based API.** Instead of decorating functions with `@Endpoint`, you create a `runpod.App` and attach resources to it with `@app.queue`, `@app.api`, or the new `@app.task`.
- **A separate runtime.** The code that runs on workers now ships in its own package, `runpod-sdk-runtime`, so it can be released independently of the SDK. See [Runtime](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/runtime).
- **A new major version.** The unified SDK is `runpod` 2.0. Version 2.0 includes breaking changes, such as the removal of the old `runpod config`, `runpod project`, and `runpod exec` CLI commands.

## What stays the same

- `runpod.Endpoint("ENDPOINT_ID")` and its `run`, `run_sync`, `status`, and `output` methods work exactly as before.
- `runpod.serverless.start` and the rest of the Serverless worker SDK are unchanged.
- API wrapper functions such as `runpod.create_pod` and `runpod.get_pods` still work.
- Your credentials file and `RUNPOD_API_KEY` carry over, so you don't need to create a new API key.

## Do you need to migrate?

Flash keeps working after its [deprecation date](https://docs.runpod.io/flash/overview), but it stops getting fixes and updates. Plan to move to the Runpod SDK by then.

Migrate if you want features that are only in the Runpod SDK:

- `@app.task` for running one ephemeral Pod per call, such as training or fine-tuning jobs.
- `runpod.Secret` for reading environment values from Runpod secrets.
- `runpod.Model` for platform-cached model weights.
- `.spawn()` and `.stream()` for background jobs and streamed results.
- `rp logs` for following a Pod's logs from your terminal.

Stay on Flash for now if your project relies on a pattern that doesn't work the same way in the Runpod SDK yet. See [Known differences](#known-differences) before you start.

## Requirements

- An existing Flash project.
- [Python 3.10 to 3.14](https://www.python.org/downloads/).
- The `runpod` package, version 2.0 or later.
- A [Runpod account](https://docs.runpod.io/accounts-billing/manage-accounts) with a verified email address.

## Step 1: Install the SDK and log in

In your project's virtual environment, remove `runpod-flash` and install `runpod`:

```bash
pip uninstall runpod-flash
pip install --upgrade runpod

# If using uv:
uv remove runpod-flash
uv add 'runpod>=2'
```

Then log in:

```bash
rp login
```

If you already logged in with `flash login`, your saved credentials still work and this step updates the same `~/.runpod/config.toml` file.

| Flash                          | Runpod SDK           |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------- |
| `pip install runpod-flash`     | `pip install runpod` |
| `uv tool install runpod-flash` | `uv add runpod`      |
| `flash login`                  | `rp login`           |
| Python 3.10 to 3.13            | Python 3.10 to 3.14  |

## Step 2: Update your CLI commands

Replace `flash` commands in your scripts, Makefiles, and CI with their `rp flash` equivalents:

| Flash                                 | Runpod SDK                                                |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `flash login`                         | `rp login`                                                |
| `flash init PROJECT_NAME`             | `rp flash init PROJECT_NAME`                              |
| `flash dev`                           | `rp flash dev main.py`                                    |
| `flash build`                         | `rp flash deploy --build-only`                            |
| `flash deploy`                        | `rp flash deploy`                                         |
| `flash deploy --env ENVIRONMENT_NAME` | `rp flash deploy --env ENVIRONMENT_NAME`                  |
| `flash app list`                      | `rp flash app list`                                       |
| `flash env list`                      | `rp flash env list --app APP_NAME`                        |
| `flash env create ENVIRONMENT_NAME`   | `rp flash env add ENVIRONMENT_NAME`                       |
| `flash undeploy ENDPOINT_NAME`        | `rp flash undeploy --app APP_NAME --env ENVIRONMENT_NAME` |
| `flash update`                        | `rp update`                                               |
| No equivalent                         | `rp logs POD_ID --follow`                                 |
| No equivalent                         | `rp secret add` and `rp registry add`                     |

See the [CLI reference](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/cli) for all commands and flags.

## Step 3: Update your code

The Runpod SDK groups your resources into an app. Work through the sections below in order.

### Imports and the app

Replace the `runpod_flash` import with `runpod` and create an app. The app name groups your resources when you deploy.

| Flash                                        | Runpod SDK                     |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `from runpod_flash import Endpoint, GpuType` | `import runpod`                |
| The project folder is the app                | `app = runpod.App("APP_NAME")` |

### Queue-based endpoints

Replace the `@Endpoint` decorator with `@app.queue`:

```python Flash
import asyncio
from runpod_flash import Endpoint, GpuType

@Endpoint(
    name="hello-gpu",
    gpu=GpuType.NVIDIA_GEFORCE_RTX_4090,
    dependencies=["torch"],
)
async def hello():
    import torch
    return {"gpu": torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}

print(asyncio.run(hello()))
```

```python Runpod SDK
import runpod

app = runpod.App("hello-gpu")

@app.queue(gpu="4090", dependencies=["torch"])
def hello():
    import torch
    return {"gpu": torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}

@runpod.local_entrypoint
def main():
    print(hello.remote())
```

Run the new version with `rp flash dev main.py`.

Resource names come from the function or class name, so the example above creates a resource called `hello`. To use a different name, pass `name=`, for example `@app.queue(name="hello-gpu", gpu="4090")`.

### Load-balanced endpoints

This is the biggest change. In Flash, you created an `Endpoint` instance and attached route functions to it. In the Runpod SDK, you write a class and mark it with `@app.api`. Methods marked with `@runpod.get` or `@runpod.post` become routes, and a method marked with `@runpod.init` runs once when each worker starts.

```python Flash
from runpod_flash import Endpoint

api = Endpoint(name="my-api", cpu="cpu3c-1-2", workers=(1, 3))

@api.get("/health")
async def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}

@api.post("/compute")
async def compute(data: dict) -> dict:
    return {"result": data}
```

```python Runpod SDK
import runpod

app = runpod.App("my-api")

@app.api(cpu="cpu3c-1-2", workers=(1, 3))
class MyApi:
    @runpod.init
    def setup(self):
        # Runs once per worker before it takes traffic
        self.ready = True

    @runpod.get("/health")
    async def health(self):
        return {"status": "ok"}

    @runpod.post("/compute")
    async def compute(self, body: dict):
        return {"result": body}
```

Workers keep state on the class instance between requests. In a dev session, call routes through the class, for example `MyApi.post("/compute", {"x": 1})`.

### Calling functions

| Flash                                                    | Runpod SDK                                                                 |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `await my_function(x)`                                   | `my_function.remote(x)`                                                    |
| Async call inside async code                             | `await my_function.remote.aio(x)`                                          |
| `asyncio.gather(...)` to start work in the background    | `job = my_function.spawn(x)` returns a `Job` immediately                   |
| No equivalent                                            | `my_function.stream(x)` yields results as they're produced                 |
| No equivalent                                            | `my_function.local(x)` runs the function in your local process             |
| `if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main())`         | Mark `main` with `@runpod.local_entrypoint` and run `rp flash dev main.py` |
| Calling another endpoint through the deployment manifest | Call it directly with `.remote()` from inside a remote function            |

### Hardware

The `GpuType` and `GpuGroup` names are the same, and you can also use shorter strings:

| Flash                                            | Runpod SDK                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `gpu=GpuType.NVIDIA_GEFORCE_RTX_4090`            | `gpu="4090"` or `gpu=runpod.GpuType.NVIDIA_GEFORCE_RTX_4090` |
| `gpu=GpuGroup.ANY`                               | `gpu=runpod.GpuGroup.ANY`                                    |
| `gpu=[GpuType.A, GpuType.B]`                     | `gpu=["H100", "A100"]` (any of the listed GPUs)              |
| `cpu="cpu5c-4-8"` or `CpuInstanceType.CPU5C_4_8` | `cpu="cpu5c-4-8"`                                            |
| `gpu_count=2`                                    | `gpu_count=2`                                                |

### Storage

| Flash                                                    | Runpod SDK                                                                |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `NetworkVolume(name="models", size=100, datacenter=...)` | `runpod.NetworkVolume("models", size=100, datacenter=...)`                |
| `volume=vol`                                             | `mounts={"/runpod-volume": vol}`                                          |
| `volume=[vol_us, vol_eu]` across datacenters             | Not supported. Use one volume per resource.                               |
| No equivalent                                            | `runpod.GlobalVolume("name")` for storage that isn't tied to a datacenter |
| Files at `/runpod-volume/`                               | Read `vol.path` inside the remote function                                |

Queue-based and load-balanced resources support one volume, mounted at `/runpod-volume`. Tasks support one network volume and one global volume at different paths. Global volumes require GPU compute.

### Other settings

| Flash                                                                                                                                                           | Runpod SDK                                                              |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `template=PodTemplate(containerDiskInGb=100)`                                                                                                                   | `container_disk_gb=100`                                                 |
| `PodTemplate(min_cuda_version="12.8")`                                                                                                                          | `min_cuda_version="12.8"` on the decorator                              |
| `python_version="3.12"` on a resource                                                                                                                           | `rp flash deploy --python-version 3.12` (defaults to your local Python) |
| `idle_timeout`, `execution_timeout_ms`, `flashboot`, `scaler_type`, `scaler_value`, `accelerate_downloads`, `datacenter`, `dependencies`, `system_dependencies` | Same names on the decorator                                             |
| No equivalent                                                                                                                                                   | `max_concurrency=4` to process several requests per worker              |

See [Resource parameters](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/configuration/parameters) for the full list.

### Environment variables and secrets

You can still pass plain values in `env`. To keep tokens out of your code, store them as Runpod secrets and reference them with `runpod.Secret`:

| Flash                        | Runpod SDK                                    |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `env={"HF_TOKEN": "hf_..."}` | `env={"HF_TOKEN": runpod.Secret("hf-token")}` |

### Existing endpoints and custom images

| Flash                                                                                | Runpod SDK                                                    |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Endpoint(id="ENDPOINT_ID")` with `await ep.run(...)` and `EndpointJob`              | `runpod.Endpoint("ENDPOINT_ID").run(...)` or `.run_sync(...)` |
| `Endpoint(name=..., image="IMAGE")` (the image must be a complete Serverless worker) | `image="IMAGE"` on any decorator (any image with Python 3)    |

## Step 4: Check behavior that changed

These differences don't raise errors, so check them before you deploy:

- **Default worker range.** Resources now default to `workers=(0, 3)` instead of `(0, 1)`, so a busy endpoint can scale to three workers. Set `workers` explicitly if you need a different limit.
- **No local server in dev sessions.** `flash dev` ran a local server on `localhost:8888` with an API explorer at `/docs`. `rp flash dev main.py` runs your `@runpod.local_entrypoint` function instead and streams worker logs to your terminal. Update any local testing that sent curl requests to `localhost:8888`.
- **Custom images work differently.** You no longer need an image that implements a Serverless handler. The SDK runs your function on any image that has Python 3.
- **One volume per endpoint.** Lists of volumes across datacenters aren't supported.
- **Volumes keep billing.** Undeploying an app doesn't delete the network volumes it created. Delete them separately when you no longer need them.
- **New ignore file.** `.flashignore` is replaced by `.runpodignore`, and deployments also follow your project's `.gitignore` files. `.env` files, keys, and credential files are always left out. See [Ignore rules](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/deploy#ignore-rules).
- **Python version must match in dev sessions.** Dev sessions and tasks send your function from your local Python, so your local interpreter must be 3.10 to 3.14. See [Dev sessions](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/apps/dev-sessions#python-version).

## Step 5: Test, then deploy

1. Run your migrated app once in a dev session and check the output:

   ```bash
   rp flash dev main.py --once
   ```

2. Fix any errors, then deploy:

   ```bash
   rp flash deploy
   ```

3. Confirm your endpoints on the [Serverless page](https://console.runpod.io/serverless) in the console.

4. When the new deployment works, remove the endpoints you deployed with Flash:

   ```bash
   flash undeploy --all
   ```

## Known differences

A few Flash patterns don't work the same way in the Runpod SDK yet. If your project uses one of them, test it carefully or stay on Flash until it's supported:

- Projects split across multiple local files.
- Classes used as remote resources, other than `@app.api` classes.
- Path and query parameters on HTTP routes.
- Resources that reference an existing template or endpoint with `template=` or `id=`.

## Flash deprecation timeline

The standalone `runpod-flash` package is deprecated. Until its deprecation date, listed on the [Flash overview](https://docs.runpod.io/flash/overview), it keeps working but gets no new features. After that date, it gets no fixes or updates. The package stays on PyPI, and Flash code and endpoints you've already deployed keep working.

The [runpod/flash](https://github.com/runpod/flash) repository will also be archived, which makes it read-only. The archive date is announced in the repository.

The Flash pages in these docs stay online for reference, with a notice pointing to the Runpod SDK docs.

### Deprecation notice

`runpod-flash` 1.21.0 and later print a deprecation notice once per process:

- The `flash` CLI prints it to stderr on every command, including `flash --help`. Output on stdout, such as from `flash --version`, is unchanged.
- The Python package raises a `FutureWarning` the first time your code uses the Flash API, such as `from runpod_flash import Endpoint`.
- Deployed Flash workers don't show the notice, so it doesn't appear in your endpoint logs.

To hide the notice, for example in CI, set `RUNPOD_FLASH_SILENCE_DEPRECATION=1`:

```bash
export RUNPOD_FLASH_SILENCE_DEPRECATION=1
```

You can also filter the warning with Python's standard warning filters, such as `PYTHONWARNINGS=ignore::FutureWarning`.

# Document: Overview

Source path: flash/overview.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/flash/overview.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/flash/overview
Description: Build autoscaling AI/ML apps using local code with Runpod Flash. Review setup, configuration, deployment, and usage guidance for Runpod Flash.

# Overview

Build autoscaling AI/ML apps using local code with Runpod Flash. Review setup, configuration, deployment, and usage guidance for Runpod Flash.

> **Warning**
>
> Flash is now part of the [Runpod SDK](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/overview). This page documents the standalone `runpod-flash` package, which gets no fixes or updates after its deprecation date, **October 29, 2026**. For new projects, use the [Runpod SDK](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/overview). To see how Flash commands and imports map to the SDK, see [Migrating from Flash](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/migrate-from-flash).

Flash is a Python SDK for developing cloud-native AI apps where you define everything—hardware, remote functions, and dependencies—using local code.

```python
import asyncio
from runpod_flash import Endpoint, GpuType

# Mark the function below for remote execution
@Endpoint(name="hello-gpu", gpu=GpuType.NVIDIA_GEFORCE_RTX_4090, dependencies=["torch"]) 
async def hello(): # This function runs on Runpod
    import torch
    gpu_name = torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)
    print(f"Hello from your GPU! ({gpu_name})")
    return {"gpu": gpu_name}

asyncio.run(hello())
print("Done!") # This runs locally
```

Write `@Endpoint` decorated Python functions on your local machine. Run them, and Flash automatically handles GPU/CPU provisioning and worker scaling on [Runpod Serverless](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/overview).

## Get started

- [Quickstart](https://docs.runpod.io/flash/quickstart)

  Write a Flash script for instant access to Runpod GPUs.
- [Create endpoints](https://docs.runpod.io/flash/create-endpoints)

  Learn how to create endpoints of various types.
- [Examples](https://github.com/runpod/flash-examples)

  Browse example Flash scripts and apps on GitHub.

## Setup

> **Note**
>
> Flash requires a Runpod account with a verified email address.

### Install Flash

> **Note**
>
> Flash requires [Python 3.10 to 3.14](https://www.python.org/downloads/) and runs natively on macOS and Linux. Windows users can run Flash through [WSL2](https://docs.runpod.io/flash/windows-wsl2).

Install Flash using `pip` or `uv`:

```bash
# Install with pip
pip install runpod-flash

# Or uv
uv tool install runpod-flash
```

### Authentication

Before you can use Flash, you need to authenticate with your Runpod account:

```bash
flash login

# If using uv:
uv run flash login
```

This saves your API key securely and allows you to use the Flash CLI and run `@Endpoint` functions.

### Coding agent integration (optional)

Install the Flash skill package for AI coding agents like Claude Code, Cline, and Cursor:

```bash
npx skills add runpod/runpod-plugins-official
```

You can review the `SKILL.md` file in the [runpod/runpod-plugins-official repository](https://github.com/runpod/runpod-plugins-official/blob/main/plugins/runpod/skills/flash/SKILL.md).

## Flash apps

When you're ready to move beyond scripts and build a production-ready API, you can create a [Flash app](https://docs.runpod.io/flash/apps/overview) (a collection of interconnected endpoints with diverse hardware configurations) and deploy it to Runpod.

[Follow this tutorial to build your first Flash app](https://docs.runpod.io/flash/apps/build-app).

## Flash CLI

The Flash CLI provides a set of commands for managing your Flash apps and endpoints.

```bash
flash --help
```

[Learn more about the Flash CLI](https://docs.runpod.io/flash/cli/overview).

## Limitations

- Flash runs natively on macOS and Linux. Windows users can run Flash through [WSL2](https://docs.runpod.io/flash/windows-wsl2).
- CPU endpoints are restricted to the `EU-RO-1` datacenter. GPU endpoints can deploy to [multiple datacenters](https://docs.runpod.io/flash/configuration/parameters#datacenter).
- Flash can rapidly scale workers across multiple endpoints, and you may hit your maximum worker threshold quickly. Contact [Runpod support](https://www.runpod.io/contact) to increase your account's capacity if needed.
