`id`, `name`, `gpu_count`, `gpu_type_id`, `status`, and `created_at` keep their names. The `desired_status`, `machine_id`, and `machine_type` attributes are gone; the 1.x data source could never populate them, so no configuration depended on them.

2.0.0 adds `cloud`, `data_center_id`, `started_at`, `locked`, `registry`, `actions`, `cpu_type_id`, `cpu_vcpu_count`, `gpu_vcpu_count`, `cuda_version`, the `global_networking` fields, `mounts.network`, `runtime` (CPU, memory, and per-GPU utilization), `ssh.direct` and `ssh.proxy`, and `cluster`.

### runpod\_machine and runpod\_machines

Both data sources remain available on the GraphQL API as deprecated shims. Each keeps its name, its required inputs, and every attribute name. As in 1.x, `data_center_id` is always null on `runpod_machine`, because the underlying query does not select it; use `runpod_machines` when you need the data center.

### runpod\_gpu\_types

The `runpod_gpu_types` data source is now read from the v2 catalog API. The list attribute is still `gpu_types`, and its nested fields were renamed to the catalog's names:

| 1.x attribute                 | 2.0.0 attribute               | Note                   |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `gpu_types[].display_name`    | `gpu_types[].name`            | Renamed.               |
| `gpu_types[].memory_in_gb`    | `gpu_types[].memory`          | Renamed. VRAM in GB.   |
| `gpu_types[].secure_cloud`    | `gpu_types[].secure`          | Renamed.               |
| `gpu_types[].secure_price`    | `gpu_types[].price_secure`    | Renamed. USD per hour. |
| `gpu_types[].community_price` | `gpu_types[].price_community` | Renamed. USD per hour. |

`gpu_types[].id` keeps its name. The `cuda_cores` and `manufacturer` fields are gone, because the v2 catalog does not carry them. 2.0.0 adds `gpu_types[].community` (availability on Community Cloud) and `gpu_types[].pool` (the Serverless pool id for `runpod_serverless_endpoint.gpu_pools`). A new single-item companion, `runpod_gpu_type`, looks up one entry by `id`.

### runpod\_data\_centers

The `runpod_data_centers` data source is now read from the v2 catalog API. The list attribute is still `data_centers`:

| 1.x attribute             | 2.0.0 attribute         | Note     |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------- | -------- |
| `data_centers[].location` | `data_centers[].region` | Renamed. |

`data_centers[].id`, `data_centers[].name`, and `data_centers[].global_network` keep their names. 2.0.0 adds `data_centers[].compliance` (compliance certifications held) and `data_centers[].network_volume_types` (storage tiers offered). A new single-item companion, `runpod_data_center`, looks up one entry by `id`.

### runpod\_template

The `runpod_template` data source keeps its name and required `id`, and mirrors the resource's renames. `image_name` becomes `image`, `container_disk_in_gb` becomes `disk`, `is_public` becomes `public`, `is_serverless` becomes `serverless`, and `container_registry_auth_id` becomes `registry`. `docker_start_cmd` becomes `args`, reshaped from a list to a single string. `volume_in_gb` and `volume_mount_path` move into `mounts.persistent.size` and `mounts.persistent.path`. `docker_entrypoint` keeps its name and is read from the v2 template. `readme`, `earned`, `is_runpod`, and `runtime_in_min` are deprecated read-only values from GraphQL. 2.0.0 adds `allowed_cuda_versions`, `start_ssh`, and `start_jupyter`.

### runpod\_container\_registry\_auths

The 2.0.0 equivalent is **`runpod_registries`**: the data source was renamed, and its list attribute `container_registry_auths` became `registries`. The `id` and `name` nested fields keep their names. `registries[].username` is deprecated and always null. REST v2 treats the username as write-only, and no other supported API reports it. The `password`, `created_at`, and `updated_at` fields are gone. They existed only in 1.0.9, which never ran, and the v2 list doesn't return them.

### runpod\_ecr\_delegations

The 2.0.0 equivalent is **`runpod_registry_delegations`**: the data source was renamed along with the resource, and its list attribute `ecr_delegations` became `delegations`. The nested `id`, `name`, `aws_user`, `aws_region`, `repository`, `tag`, `docker_registry_uri`, and `created_at` fields keep their names. The `resource` field is gone, because the API does not echo the delegated ARN; read it from your own configuration. 2.0.0 adds `delegations[].delegator_user_id`, the Runpod user that created the delegation.

### runpod\_user

The `runpod_user` data source is kept as a deprecated shim. It now reads the GraphQL `myself` query, because the REST v1 `/user` route is gone. Every attribute keeps its name, but only `id` and `email` have a source. The others read null.

### runpod\_endpoint\_workers

The `runpod_endpoint_workers` data source keeps its name and required `endpoint_id`, with richer per-worker data and a status summary:

| 1.x attribute          | 2.0.0 attribute            | Note                                                        |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `workers[].start_time` | `workers[].started_at`     | Renamed. RFC 3339.                                          |
| `workers[].uptime_ms`  | `workers[].uptime_seconds` | Renamed, and the unit changed from milliseconds to seconds. |

`workers[].id` and `workers[].status` keep their names. The synthetic top-level `id`, along with `workers[].pod_id` and `workers[].last_busy_ms`, are gone, because the v2 worker list does not carry them. 2.0.0 adds per-worker `data_center_id`, `gpu_type_id`, `gpu_count`, `image`, and `is_stale`, plus a `summary` of counts by status and the endpoint's current `endpoint_version`.

### runpod\_endpoint\_worker\_logs

The `runpod_endpoint_worker_logs` data source keeps its name and required `endpoint_id` and `worker_id`. The API serves logs as a live event stream. A read collects what the stream delivers and ends when the API closes it or the provider's 60-second timeout elapses. The `logs` attribute (one string) became `lines` (a list of line strings); use `join` to get the old shape. The synthetic `id` is gone. 2.0.0 adds `entries` (per-event `line`, `timestamp`, and `source`) and the `tail`, `since`, `last_event_id`, and `source` arguments to bound the read.

### Billing data sources

The three 1.x billing data sources still exist in 2.0.0. They're deprecated and keep their 1.x names, arguments, and record fields, but they now read the v2 billing routes and map each record back into the 1.x shape, so some records differ from 1.x. See [Deprecated shims](#deprecated-shims). New configuration should use the v2-native equivalents below, which report cost components in USD. The record shape changed, so moving to them is a rewrite rather than a rename. In every case the `billing_records` list became `records`, `billing_records[].amount` became `records[].amounts.total_amount`, and the single `time` field became a `start_time` and `end_time` pair on each record. Each data source also adds a `last_n` argument and a `metadata` block. The `last_n` argument returns the last N buckets and is mutually exclusive with an explicit window. The `metadata` block describes the resolved window and its totals.

| 1.x data source                 | 2.0.0 data source               | Note                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `runpod_billing_pod`            | `runpod_pod_billing`            | Adds `records[].amounts.gpu_amount`, `.cpu_amount`, and `.disk_amount`. The `gpu_type_id` filter, `time_billed_ms`, `disk_space_billed_gb`, and the record's `endpoint_id` have no 2.0.0 equivalent. |
| `runpod_billing_network_volume` | `runpod_network_volume_billing` | Adds per-tier `records[].amounts.standard_amount` and `.high_performance_amount`. `time_billed_ms` and `disk_space_billed_gb` have no 2.0.0 equivalent.                                              |
| `runpod_billing_endpoint`       | `runpod_serverless_billing`     | The `endpoint_id` filter became `serverless_id`. `time_billed_ms` has no 2.0.0 equivalent.                                                                                                           |

> **Warning**
>
> Watch the name on the endpoint billing move. 1.x `runpod_billing_endpoint` reported spend on your Serverless endpoints, and its 2.0.0 replacement is `runpod_serverless_billing`. The similarly named `runpod_endpoint_billing` in 2.0.0 is a different data source that reports spend on Runpod's own Public Endpoints. Do not map to it by name.

### Removed data sources

`runpod_endpoint_jobs` and `runpod_endpoint_job_logs` have no 2.0.0 equivalent, because jobs and their logs live on the Serverless runtime API. For worker-level output, use `runpod_endpoint_worker_logs`, and for Pod output, use the new `runpod_pod_logs`.

## New in 2.0.0

2.0.0 adds capabilities that 1.x had no surface for.

**Clusters** are multi-node groups of identical Pods on one private overlay network, with SLURM, Ray, training, and application topologies. Read them with `runpod_cluster`, `runpod_clusters`, and `runpod_cluster_pods`.

```hcl
resource "runpod_cluster" "training" {
  name              = "llama-finetune"
  type              = "SLURM"
  gpu_type_id       = "NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3"
  gpu_count_per_pod = 8
  pod_count         = 4
  image             = "runpod/pytorch:2.8.0-py3.11-cuda12.8.1-cudnn-devel-ubuntu22.04"
}
```

**Global volumes** are usage-billed storage with no data center. A Pod mounts one through `global_volumes` wherever it's placed, and a GPU Serverless endpoint mounts one on every worker through its own `global_volumes`. Read one with the `runpod_global_volume` data source.

```hcl
resource "runpod_global_volume" "data" {
  name = "training-data"
}

resource "runpod_pod" "trainer" {
  name        = "trainer"
  image       = "runpod/pytorch:2.8.0-py3.11-cuda12.8.1-cudnn-devel-ubuntu22.04"
  gpu_type_id = "NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090"

  global_volumes = [{ volume_id = runpod_global_volume.data.id, path = "/data" }]
}
```

**Account SSH keys** manage the account's registered public keys as a singleton. Every write replaces the whole document, so declare it once per account.

```hcl
resource "runpod_account_ssh_keys" "this" {
  keys              = var.ssh_public_keys
  remove_on_destroy = false
}
```

**CPU Pods and CPU Serverless endpoints** replace the GPU type with a CPU flavor, taking the vCPU count from the flavor's catalog range. The flavors are in the new `runpod_cpu_type` and `runpod_cpu_types` catalog data sources.

```hcl
resource "runpod_pod" "preprocess" {
  name        = "preprocess-pod"
  image       = "runpod/pytorch:2.8.0-py3.11-cuda12.8.1-cudnn-devel-ubuntu22.04"
  cpu_type_id = "cpu5c"
  vcpu_count  = 4
}
```

**CUDA and host-size constraints** filter placement with an open-ended floor or an exact set, plus per-GPU RAM and vCPU floors on Pods.

```hcl
resource "runpod_pod" "strict" {
  name                   = "strict-pod"
  image                  = "runpod/pytorch:2.8.0-py3.11-cuda12.8.1-cudnn-devel-ubuntu22.04"
  gpu_type_id            = "NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090"
  min_cuda_version       = "12.1"
  min_ram_per_gpu        = 8
  min_vcpu_count_per_gpu = 2
}
```

2.0.0 also adds these data sources and settings:

- **Catalog templates**: the publicly shared template catalog, read through `runpod_catalog_templates`.
- **Serverless builds and releases**: `runpod_endpoint_builds` and `runpod_endpoint_build` report container builds from a Git repository, and `runpod_endpoint_releases` reports configuration releases with a field-level diff against the previous one.
- **Billing on the v2 routes**: `runpod_billing` (account-wide), `runpod_pod_billing`, `runpod_serverless_billing`, `runpod_endpoint_billing`, `runpod_network_volume_billing`, and `runpod_cluster_billing`, all with the same window arguments and per-component totals.
- **List data sources**: `runpod_pods`, `runpod_templates`, `runpod_serverless_endpoints`, and `runpod_network_volumes` read every resource of that kind on the account.
- **Pod logs**: `runpod_pod_logs`, the Pod-level counterpart to worker logs, bounded by `tail`, `since`, or `last_event_id`.
- **Single-item catalog lookups**: `runpod_gpu_type`, `runpod_cpu_type`, and `runpod_data_center`, so you no longer filter a whole list to read one entry.
- **FlashBoot tiers**: cold-start acceleration is now a three-value setting (`OFF`, `FLASHBOOT`, or `PRIORITY_FLASHBOOT`) rather than a boolean.
- **Declarative Pod run state**: `runpod_pod.desired_state` (`RUNNING` or `EXITED`) makes a Pod stopped outside Terraform show up as a plan diff and get started again on the next apply.

## Removed in 2.0.0

Some 1.x attributes are gone in 2.0.0. Most of them were declared in the 1.x schema but never sent to the service, so removing them changes no behavior.

- **Spot Pods** (`type = "SPOT"`, `interruptible`, and `bid_per_gpu`) were retired by the platform. The APIs stopped accepting bids, so migrate these configurations to on-demand Pods.
- **`stop_after`, `terminate_after`, `port`, and `volume_key` on `runpod_pod`** were schema-only in 1.x and have no v2 counterpart. Use `desired_state` or `runpod_pod_action` for a scheduled stop or terminate, declare ports as a list in `ports`, and note that the v2 API has no volume encryption key.
- **Machine pinning on Pods** never worked in 1.x, and the v2 Pod create has no machine parameter. Constrain placement with `data_center_ids` and the per-GPU RAM and vCPU floors instead.
- **`cloud_type` on endpoints, and `password`, `created_at`, and `updated_at` on the registry list** existed only in 1.0.9, which never ran. They were never in 1.0.8.

## Deprecated shims

A shim is a small piece of code inside the provider that keeps a 1.x feature working when REST v2 has no equivalent yet. For a runnable example, see [Legacy shims](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/runpod/runpod/latest/docs/guides/legacy) on the Terraform Registry.

Everything a 1.0.8 configuration used that REST v2 has no field for still plans in 2.0.0, marked deprecated. Where only GraphQL has the value, the provider reads or writes it there through `graphql_url`. Where no API has the value anymore, the attribute is kept so the configuration still plans, and it reads null or isn't applied. Terraform prints a deprecation warning on every plan that touches a shim, and each shim is removed in a later release once REST v2 covers it.

2.0.0 makes no REST v1 calls, so the REST v1 retirement on November 15, 2026 doesn't affect any shim.

| 1.x attribute                                                         | 2.0.0 reads it from        | What you see                                                                                                                                    |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `runpod_pod.machine_id`                                               | GraphQL                    | The machine id; null when GraphQL doesn't report the Pod.                                                                                       |
| `runpod_pod.volume_encrypted`                                         | GraphQL                    | `false` for an unencrypted volume, not null.                                                                                                    |
| `runpod_template.readme`                                              | GraphQL (write and read)   | Written and read as before. `""` is refused, so the text can't be cleared.                                                                      |
| `runpod_template.earned`, `is_runpod`, `runtime_in_min`               | GraphQL                    | Same as 1.x. `earned` and `runtime_in_min` read 0 for a template the account doesn't own.                                                       |
| `runpod_serverless_endpoint.gpu_type_priority`, `cpu_flavor_priority` | Nothing                    | Kept in state, never sent, warned about at plan time.                                                                                           |
| `runpod_serverless_endpoint.template_version`                         | Nothing                    | Always null.                                                                                                                                    |
| `runpod_serverless_endpoint.users`                                    | GraphQL                    | The owner, as a one-element list.                                                                                                               |
| `runpod_serverless_endpoint.version` and `workers`                    | REST v2 workers listing    | Same as 1.x, except `workers[].last_busy_ms` is always null and `uptime_ms` has whole-second precision.                                         |
| `runpod_billing_pod` with `gpu_type_id`                               | GraphQL GPU Pod billing    | Per GPU type, as in 1.x. Can't be combined with `pod_id`. Hourly buckets over 13 days old and other buckets over 13 months old aren't reported. |
| `runpod_billing_pod` without `gpu_type_id`                            | REST v2                    | One record per Pod, where 1.x grouped by GPU type. `gpu_type_id`, `endpoint_id`, `disk_space_billed_gb`, and `time_billed_ms` read null.        |
| `runpod_billing_network_volume`                                       | REST v2                    | One record per volume, where 1.x reported the whole account. `disk_space_billed_gb` and `time_billed_ms` read null.                             |
| `runpod_billing_endpoint` `time_billed_ms`                            | GraphQL Serverless billing | Whole-second precision. Null for yearly buckets, hourly buckets over 13 days old, and other buckets over 13 months old.                         |
| `runpod_registries.registries[].username`                             | Nothing                    | Always null.                                                                                                                                    |

The `runpod_machine` resource, the `runpod_machine` and `runpod_machines` data sources, and the `runpod_user` data source also run on GraphQL. Only `id` and `email` are populated on `runpod_user`.

For the three billing data sources, `end_time` must be an RFC 3339 timestamp, a date, or a datetime without a zone (read as UTC). The window is the 30 days before `end_time`, or before the current time when it's unset.

When GraphQL fails, an unconfigured shim attribute reads null with a warning and the apply goes through. A shim attribute your configuration sets fails the apply. The billing data sources always fail on a bad read.

`compute_type` on `runpod_serverless_endpoint` is deprecated for a different reason. It restates what `gpu_pools` or `cpu` already says, and it goes away once 1.x configurations have moved, not when an API changes.

Don't build new configuration on any shim.

## State migration

2.0.0 ships no state upgraders. Every resource schema is at version 0 in both majors. Terraform does not rewrite a 1.x state entry into the 2.0.0 shape. Wherever the attribute set changed, the old entry cannot be decoded and must be removed and re-imported. `terraform state rm` and `terraform import` change state only: running them stops no Pod and deletes no volume. Do the state work after rewriting the configuration and before the first `terraform apply`.

### Before importing a Pod you want to keep

> **Warning**
>
> The v2 Pod read does not return eight create-time attributes: `template_id`, `start_ssh`, `start_jupyter`, `allowed_cuda_versions`, `min_cuda_version`, `min_ram_per_gpu`, `min_vcpu_count_per_gpu`, and `data_center_ids`. A 2.0.0 Pod configuration can set all eight. After `terraform import`, each one the configuration sets shows as a diff on the first plan, and all eight force replacement. Applying that plan deletes the Pod permanently, along with everything not on a network volume, and creates a new Pod with a new id. The "after" Pod example in this guide sets `start_ssh` and `start_jupyter`, so a Pod migrated with it as written would be replaced.

There are two safe ways through:

- **Leave a running 1.x Pod on 1.x.** Do not remove and import it. Keep it in a root module pinned to `version = "<= 1.0.8"`. Don't use `~> 1.0`, which selects 1.0.9. That release can't serve its own schema or configure most of its resources. Let that provider manage it until the Pod is due to be recreated anyway. Then create its successor under 2.0.0.
- **Adopt it with `ignore_changes`.** If the Pod has to move to 2.0.0 now, add a `lifecycle` block before the first apply. Name every one of the eight attributes the configuration sets. Listing all eight is harmless if you are unsure which the Pod was created with.

```hcl
resource "runpod_pod" "training" {
  # ...
  start_ssh     = true
  start_jupyter = true

  lifecycle {
    ignore_changes = [start_ssh, start_jupyter]
  }
}
```

The cost of `ignore_changes` is that Terraform never enforces those values on this Pod. State keeps them empty, so changing one later plans nothing at all. To apply a new value, take the attribute out of `ignore_changes` and accept the replacement. On a GPU Pod, also set `cloud` and `gpu_count` to the values the Pod already has. Leaving either out makes any other change plan as unknown, and both force replacement. Also, an import reads the Pod's whole environment into state, so the first apply that sets `env` removes every key the configuration leaves out, including keys that came from a template. The plan lists those removals.

Either way, read the first plan before applying it. It must not replace a Pod you mean to keep, and the `# forces replacement` marker names the attribute responsible.

### Re-import with the same type name

The type name does not change, and the id is the one you already have. The attribute set still changed, though, so remove and import each resource. This applies to `runpod_pod`, `runpod_template`, `runpod_network_volume`, and `runpod_machine`. For `runpod_machine`, the attribute names are unchanged, but re-import anyway because the resource is a different implementation.

```bash
terraform state rm runpod_pod.training
terraform import runpod_pod.training pod_abc123
```

### Re-import with a renamed type

The old address cannot be read once 2.0.0 is in the lock file, because the type no longer exists. `terraform state mv` does not help either, because the type is part of the address and the schemas differ. Remove the old address, then import the new one against the same id. This applies to `runpod_endpoint`, which becomes `runpod_serverless_endpoint`.

```bash
terraform state rm runpod_endpoint.inference
terraform import runpod_serverless_endpoint.inference ep_abc123
```

### Recreate a renamed type that cannot be imported

The credential and delegation types were renamed, and neither can be imported, because the v2 API does not return the values needed to reconstruct them. Remove the old address and let the new resource be created; it gets a new id, so update every `registry` reference on Pods and endpoints. The 1.x resource stays on the account until you delete it in the console. This applies to `runpod_container_registry_auth`, which becomes `runpod_registry`, and `runpod_ecr_delegation`, which becomes `runpod_registry_delegation`.

```bash
terraform state rm runpod_container_registry_auth.private
terraform apply
```

### Remove and re-declare

`runpod_pod_action` holds no Pod state and cannot be imported, so remove the old address and re-declare it.

> **Warning**
>
> Re-declaring `runpod_pod_action` runs the action again on create, so a `terminate` action you re-declare will terminate the Pod. If you wanted a persistent run state, drop the resource and set `runpod_pod.desired_state` instead. If you wanted a one-off, add a `triggers` map so future runs are deliberate.

### Remove with nothing to import

The `runpod_endpoint_job` and `runpod_endpoint_worker` resource types are gone, so remove them from state:

```bash
terraform state rm runpod_endpoint_job.warmup
terraform state rm runpod_endpoint_worker.pinned
```

The account SSH keys singleton, new in 2.0.0, imports by the literal id `account`.

### Final check

After the state work, run `terraform plan`. Expect:

- No changes for templates, network volumes, endpoints, and machines.
- For each imported Pod, no replacement, and at most an in-place update for the `env` and `desired_state` that an import leaves empty.
- A create for each registry credential and delegation.
- A refresh on the log, worker, and billing data sources.

A planned Pod replacement has one of two causes. One is a create-time attribute the Pod guidance above says to cover. The other is a configuration mismatch against what the API reports, shown by the `# forces replacement` marker. Fix the configuration rather than applying it.

## Next steps

- Review the [provider reference on the Terraform Registry](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/runpod/runpod/latest/docs) for every 2.0.0 argument and attribute.
- Read [Manage Runpod infrastructure with Terraform](https://docs.runpod.io/integrations/terraform/overview) for authentication options and the APIs the provider calls.


# Document: Overview

Source path: hub/overview.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/hub/overview.mdx

Description: Discover, deploy, and share preconfigured AI repos using the Runpod Hub. Review publishing and management guidance for the Runpod Hub.

# Overview

Discover, deploy, and share preconfigured AI repos using the Runpod Hub. Review publishing and management guidance for the Runpod Hub.

The [Runpod Hub](https://console.runpod.io/hub) is a centralized repository for discovering, sharing, and deploying preconfigured AI repos optimized for Serverless and Pod infrastructure.

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/runpod/docs/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/images/hub-homepage.png)

## Why use the Hub?

**For users:**

- **Production-ready solutions**: Vetted, open-source repos with minimal setup required.
- **One-click deployment**: Go from discovery to running services in minutes.
- **Configurable**: Customize parameters without diving into code.

**For creators:**

- **Showcase your work**: Share projects with the AI community.
- **Automated pipeline**: The Hub builds and tests your releases automatically.
- **Earn revenue**: Generate up to 7% of compute revenue when users deploy your repos. See [revenue sharing](https://docs.runpod.io/hub/revenue-sharing).

## Public Endpoints

The Hub also offers Public Endpoints for popular AI models. These are ready-to-use APIs with instant access, interactive playgrounds, and usage-based pricing. Browse available models in the [model reference](https://docs.runpod.io/public-endpoints/reference).

## Deploy a repo

1. Go to the [Hub](https://www.console.runpod.io/hub) and select a repo.
2. Review hardware requirements and configuration options.
3. Click **Deploy** → **Create Endpoint**.

Your endpoint will be ready for integration within minutes.

1. Go to the [Hub](https://www.console.runpod.io/hub) and select a repo.
2. Click **Deploy**, select **Pod** as the deployment type.
3. Click **Deploy Pod**.

After deployment, find a sample request in the Pod details pane:

```python
import requests

response = requests.post(
    'https://POD_ID-80.proxy.runpod.net/v2/LOCAL/run',
    headers={
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'Authorization': 'Bearer YOUR_API_KEY'
    },
    json={'input': {"prompt": "Your prompt"}}
)
```

## Publish your own repo

Publish your GitHub repository on the Hub by preparing a worker with a handler function and `Dockerfile`.

> **Tip**
>
> New to building Serverless workers? Follow the [quickstart guide](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/quickstart).

1. Add configuration files in a `.runpod` directory per the [publishing guide](https://docs.runpod.io/hub/publishing-guide).
2. Create a GitHub release.
3. Submit your repository through the Runpod console.
4. After review and approval, your repo appears in the Hub.

Once published, earn revenue from user deployments. Link your GitHub profile to your Runpod account for verified maintainer status. Revenue tiers range from 1% (100-999 compute hours) to 7% (10,000+ hours), paid monthly as Runpod credits.

## How Hub repos work

1. **Repository integration**: Connects with GitHub repos using releases (not commits) for versioning.
2. **Configuration**: Repos use `hub.json` and `tests.json` in a `.runpod` directory to define metadata and test procedures.
3. **Automated pipeline**: The Hub builds and tests repos on submission and monitors for new releases.
4. **Deployment**: Users browse, customize, and deploy with minimal configuration.


# Document: Runpod Hub publishing guide

Source path: hub/publishing-guide.mdx
Pinned source: https://github.com/runpod/docs/blob/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/hub/publishing-guide.mdx
Canonical documentation: https://docs.runpod.io/hub/publishing-guide
Description: Publish your repositories to the Runpod Hub. Review setup, publishing, and management guidance for resources in the Runpod Hub.

# Runpod Hub publishing guide

Publish your repositories to the Runpod Hub. Review setup, publishing, and management guidance for resources in the Runpod Hub.

Learn how to publish your repositories to the [Runpod Hub](https://console.runpod.io/hub), including how to configure your repository with the required `hub.json` and `tests.json` files.

After you publish your repository to the Hub, you can start [earning revenue](https://docs.runpod.io/hub/revenue-sharing) from your users' compute usage.

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/runpod/docs/c845f73c104cb4b69f4caa11f27180533ad8546f/images/hub-publish-page.png)

## How to publish your repo

Follow these steps to add your repository to the Hub:

1. Navigate to the [Hub page](https://www.console.runpod.io/hub) in the Runpod console.
2. Under **Add your repo** click **Get Started**.
3. Enter your GitHub repo URL.
4. Follow the UI steps to add your repo to the Hub.

The Hub page will guide you through the following steps:

1. Create your `hub.json` and `tests.json` files.
2. Ensure your repository contains a `handler.py`, `Dockerfile`, and `README.md` file (in either the `.runpod` or root directory).
3. Create a new GitHub release (the Hub indexes releases, not commits).
4. (Optional) Add a Runpod Hub badge into your GitHub `README.md` file, so that users can instantly deploy your repo from GitHub.

After all the necessary files are in place and a release has been created, your repo will be marked "Pending" during building/testing. After testing is complete, the Runpod team will manually review the repo for publication.

## Update a repo

To update your repo on the Hub, just **create a new GitHub release**, and the Hub listing will be automatically indexed and built (usually within an hour).

## Required files

Aside from a working [Serverless implementation](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/overview), every Hub repo requires two additional configuration files:

1. `hub.json` - Defines metadata and deployment settings for your repo.
2. `tests.json` - Specifies how to test your repo.

These files should be placed in the `.runpod` directory at the root of your repository. This directory takes precedence over the root directory, allowing you to override common files like `Dockerfile` and `README.md` specifically for the Hub.

## hub.json reference

The `hub.json` file defines how your listing appears and functions in the Hub.

You can build your `hub.json` from scratch, or use [this template](#hubjson-template) as a starting point.

### General metadata

| Field         | Description                        | Required | Values                                                          |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `title`       | Name of your tool                  | Yes      | String                                                          |
| `description` | Brief explanation of functionality | Yes      | String                                                          |
| `type`        | Deployment type                    | Yes      | `"serverless"`                                                  |
| `category`    | Tool category                      | Yes      | `"audio"`, `"embedding"`, `"language"`, `"video"`, or `"image"` |
| `iconUrl`     | URL to tool icon                   | No       | Valid URL                                                       |
| `config`      | Runpod configuration               | Yes      | Object ([see below](#runpod-configuration))                     |

### Runpod configuration

| Field                 | Description                                                                                                                               | Required                    | Values                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `runsOn`              | Machine type                                                                                                                              | Yes                         | `"GPU"` or `"CPU"`                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `endpointType`        | Endpoint deployment type. When set to `"LB"`, users can deploy your listing as a Serverless endpoint or a Pod directly from the Hub page. | No                          | `"LB"`                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `containerDiskInGb`   | Container disk space allocation                                                                                                           | Yes                         | Integer (GB)                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `cpuFlavor`           | CPU configuration                                                                                                                         | Only if `runsOn` is `"CPU"` | Valid CPU flavor string. For a complete list of available CPU flavors, see [CPU types](https://docs.runpod.io/references/cpu-types)                                                                                        |
| `gpuCount`            | Number of GPUs                                                                                                                            | Only if `runsOn` is `"GPU"` | Integer                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `gpuIds`              | GPU pool specification                                                                                                                    | Only if `runsOn` is `"GPU"` | Comma-separated pool IDs (e.g., `"ADA_24"`) with optional GPU ID negations (e.g., `"-NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090"`).  For a list of GPU pools and IDs, see [GPU types](https://docs.runpod.io/references/gpu-types#gpu-pools). |
| `allowedCudaVersions` | Supported CUDA versions                                                                                                                   | No                          | Array of version strings                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `env`                 | Environment variable definitions                                                                                                          | No                          | Object ([see below](#environment-variables))                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `presets`             | Default environment variable values                                                                                                       | No                          | Object ([see below](#presets))                                                                                                                                                                                             |

### Environment variables

Environment variables can be defined in several ways:

1. **Static variables**: Direct value assignment. For example:

   ```json
   {
     "key": "API_KEY",
     "value": "default-api-key-value"
   }
   ```

2. **String inputs**: User-entered text fields. For example:

   ```json
   {
     "key": "MODEL_PATH",
     "input": {
       "name": "Model path",
       "type": "string",
       "description": "Path to the model weights on disk",
       "default": "/models/stable-diffusion-v1-5",
       "advanced": false
     }
   }
   ```

3. **Hugging Face inputs:** Fields for model selection from Hugging Face Hub. For example:

   ```json
   {
     "key": "HF_MODEL",
     "input": {
       "type": "huggingface",
       "name": "Hugging Face Model",
       "description": "Model organization/name as listed on Huggingface Hub",
       "default": "runwayml/stable-diffusion-v1-5",
       "required": true
     }
   }
   ```

4. **Option inputs**: User selected option fields. For example:

   ```json
   {
     "key": "PRECISION",
     "input": {
       "name": "Model precision",
       "type": "string",
       "description": "The numerical precision for model inference",
       "options": [
         {"label": "Full Precision (FP32)", "value": "fp32"},
         {"label": "Half Precision (FP16)", "value": "fp16"},
         {"label": "8-bit Quantization", "value": "int8"}
       ],
       "default": "fp16"
     }
   }
   ```

5. **Number Inputs**: User-entered numeric fields. For example:

   ```json
   {
     "key": "MAX_TOKENS",
     "input": {
       "name": "Maximum tokens",
       "type": "number",
       "description": "Maximum number of tokens to generate",
       "min": 32,
       "max": 4096,
       "default": 1024
     }
   }
   ```

6. **Boolean Inputs**: User-toggled boolean fields. For example:

   ```json
   {
     "key": "USE_FLASH_ATTENTION",
     "input": {
       "type": "boolean",
       "name": "Flash attention",
       "description": "Enable Flash Attention for faster inference on supported GPUs",
       "default": true,
       "trueValue": "true", 
       "falseValue": "false"
     }
   }
   ```

Advanced options will be hidden by default. Hide an option by setting: `"advanced": true` .

### Presets

Presets allow you to define groups of default environment variable values. When a user deploys your repo, they'll be offered a dropdown menu with any preset options you've defined.

Here are some example presets:

```json
"presets": [
  {
    "name": "Quality Optimized",
    "defaults": {
      "MODEL_NAME": "runpod-stable-diffusion-xl",
      "INFERENCE_MODE": "quality",
      "BATCH_SIZE": 1,
      "ENABLE_CACHING": false,
      "USE_FLASH_ATTENTION": true
    }
  },
  {
    "name": "Performance Optimized",
    "defaults": {
      "MODEL_NAME": "runpod-stable-diffusion-v1-5",
      "INFERENCE_MODE": "fast",
      "BATCH_SIZE": 8,
      "ENABLE_CACHING": true,
      "USE_FLASH_ATTENTION": true
    }
  }
]
```

            {"label": "Option 2", "value": "value2"}

        }

## tests.json reference

The `tests.json` file defines test cases to validate your tool's functionality. Tests are executed during the build step after a release has been created. A test is considered valid by the Hub if the endpoint returns a [200 response](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/200).

You can build your `tests.json` from scratch, or use [this template](#testsjson-template) as a starting point.

### Test cases

Each test case should include:

| Field     | Description           | Required | Values                 |
| --------- | --------------------- | -------- | ---------------------- |
| `name`    | Test identifier       | Yes      | String                 |
| `input`   | Raw job input payload | Yes      | Object                 |
| `timeout` | Max execution time    | No       | Integer (milliseconds) |

### Test environment configuration

| Field                 | Description                   | Required           | Values                                                                                 |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `gpuTypeId`           | GPU type for testing          | Only for GPU tests | Valid GPU ID (see [GPU types](https://docs.runpod.io/references/gpu-types))            |
| `gpuCount`            | Number of GPUs                | Only for GPU tests | Integer                                                                                |
| `cpuFlavor`           | CPU configuration for testing | Only for CPU tests | Valid CPU flavor string (see [CPU types](https://docs.runpod.io/references/cpu-types)) |
| `env`                 | Test environment variables    | No                 | Array of key-value pairs                                                               |
| `allowedCudaVersions` | Supported CUDA versions       | No                 | Array of version strings                                                               |

## tests.json template

Here’s an example `tests.json` file that you can use as a starting point:

```json title="tests.json"
{
  "tests": [
    {
      "name": "test_case_name",
      "input": {
        "param1": "value1",
        "param2": "value2"
      },
      "timeout": 10000
    }
  ],
  "config": {
    "gpuTypeId": "NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090",
    "gpuCount": 1,
    "env": [
      {
        "key": "TEST_ENV_VAR",
        "value": "test_value"
      }
    ],
    "allowedCudaVersions": [
      "12.7", "12.6", "12.5", "12.4",
      "12.3", "12.2", "12.1", "12.0", "11.7"
    ]
  }
}
```

Source path: hub/revenue-sharing.mdx

Description: Earn Runpod credits from your repositories published to the Runpod Hub. Review publishing and management guidance for the Runpod Hub.

# Revenue sharing

Earn Runpod credits from your repositories published to the Runpod Hub. Review publishing and management guidance for the Runpod Hub.

Starting in September 2025, every repository [published to the Runpod Hub](https://docs.runpod.io/hub/publishing-guide) automatically generates revenue for its maintainers. When users deploy your repositories from the Hub to run on Runpod infrastructure, you earn up to 7% of the compute revenue they generate, paid directly to your Runpod credit balance.

### How it works

Revenue share is calculated based on the total compute hours generated by users running your repositories each month. The percentage you earn depends on your monthly usage tier, with higher tiers offering better revenue rates.

1. Users deploy your repos: When users find and deploy your repositories from the Hub, they generate compute hours on Runpod infrastructure.
2. Usage is tracked: The platform tracks all compute hours generated by deployments of your repositories.
3. Monthly calculations: At the end of each month, your total compute hours are calculated and assigned to a revenue tier.
4. Credits deposited: Your revenue share is automatically deposited into your Runpod account balance.

### Revenue tiers

Revenue tiers reset monthly based on the total compute hours generated by all your published repositories:

- 10,000+ hours: 7% revenue share
- 5,000-9,999 hours: 5% revenue share
- 1,000-4,999 hours: 3% revenue share
- 100-999 hours: 1% revenue share
- Below 100 hours: 0% revenue share

For example, if users generate 2,500 compute hours using your repositories in a month, you would earn $75 in Runpod credits from those hours (3% of the total compute revenue).

### Requirements

To participate in the revenue sharing program, you must:

1. Link your GitHub profile: Connect your Runpod account to your GitHub profile for verified maintainer status. This ensures you receive credits for repositories you maintain.
2. Have published repositories: Your repositories must be successfully published and approved in the Hub.
3. Maintain active repositories: Keep your repositories up to date with working releases.

### Payment timing

Credits are deposited into your Runpod account balance during the first week of each month. Revenue is calculated based on the previous month's activity.


# Document: Migrate to Runpod

Description: Move GPU workloads to Runpod from another cloud or AI platform, with a step-by-step guide for each one and a coding agent skill that does the work.

# Migrate to Runpod

Move GPU workloads to Runpod from another cloud or AI platform, with a step-by-step guide for each one and a coding agent skill that does the work.

These guides take a workload that runs on another platform and land it on Runpod. Each one maps the other platform's concepts to Runpod's, lists what works differently, and walks through the move with before and after code, CLI commands, and API calls. Every guide was written against the other platform's current documentation.

> **Tip**
>
> Want an agent to do it? Install the [Runpod skills](https://docs.runpod.io/get-started/agent-skills) and ask your coding agent to migrate the project. See [Migrate with a coding agent](#migrate-with-a-coding-agent).

## Choose your guide

### GPU clouds

- [Vast.ai](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/vast-ai)

  Instances, templates, and Vast Serverless to Pods and Serverless.
- [Lambda](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/lambda)

  On-demand instances, filesystems, and 1-Click Clusters.
- [CoreWeave](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/coreweave)

  Kubernetes workloads, Slurm, and object storage.
- [Paperspace and DigitalOcean](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/paperspace)

  Machines, Notebooks, Deployments, and GPU Droplets.

### Serverless and inference platforms

- [Modal](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/modal)

  Modal apps, functions, classes, and volumes to the Runpod SDK.
- [Replicate](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/replicate)

  Hosted models, Cog models, and deployments.
- [Baseten](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/baseten)

  Truss models, Model APIs, and autoscaling settings.
- [fal](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/fal)

  Model APIs, the queue API, and fal Serverless apps.
- [Together AI](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/together-ai)

  Serverless inference, dedicated endpoints, and fine-tuned models.
- [Fireworks AI](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/fireworks-ai)

  Serverless inference, on-demand deployments, and custom models.
- [Hugging Face](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/hugging-face)

  Inference Endpoints, custom handlers, and GPU Spaces.

### Hyperscalers

- [AWS](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/aws)

  EC2 GPU instances, SageMaker, and Bedrock.
- [Google Cloud](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/google-cloud)

  Compute Engine, Vertex AI, and Cloud Run.
- [Azure](https://docs.runpod.io/migrate/azure)

  GPU VMs, Azure Machine Learning, and Azure OpenAI.

The hyperscaler guides include a Terraform path that uses the [Runpod Terraform provider](https://docs.runpod.io/integrations/terraform/overview), so you can run both providers in one configuration while you move.

### Frameworks and API versions

- [Cog](https://docs.runpod.io/tutorials/migrations/cog/overview)

  Run an existing Cog image on Runpod Serverless.
- [OpenAI](https://docs.runpod.io/tutorials/migrations/openai/overview)

  Point OpenAI client code at a vLLM endpoint on Runpod.
- [Runpod REST v1 and GraphQL](https://docs.runpod.io/api-reference-v2/migrate-from-v1)

  Move existing Runpod integrations to REST API v2.
- [Flash](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/migrate-from-flash)

  Move a `runpod-flash` project to the Runpod SDK.

If your platform isn't listed, the process below still applies. Match each workload to a Runpod product by its shape, then follow that product's docs.

## Where workloads land

The other platform's product name matters less than what the workload does. Sort each one by its shape.

| Workload                                                        | Runpod product                                                                                      | Start here                                                                           |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Calls a model someone else hosts.                               | [Public Endpoints](https://docs.runpod.io/public-endpoints/overview), when Runpod hosts that model. | [Quickstart](https://docs.runpod.io/public-endpoints/quickstart)                     |
| Takes a request, returns a response, and sits idle in between.  | [Serverless](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/overview) queue-based endpoint.                      | [Serverless quickstart](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/quickstart)                |
| Runs your own HTTP server with custom routes and low latency.   | Serverless [load-balancing endpoint](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/load-balancing/overview).    | [Load balancing overview](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/load-balancing/overview) |
| Serves an LLM behind an OpenAI-compatible API.                  | Serverless endpoint running the [vLLM worker](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/vllm/overview).     | [vLLM quickstart](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/vllm/get-started)                |
| Python functions you'd rather not containerize yourself.        | The [Runpod SDK](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/overview).                                              | [SDK quickstart](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/quickstart)                              |
| A job that runs to completion, such as training or a batch run. | A [Pod](https://docs.runpod.io/pods/overview), or one Pod per call from the Runpod SDK.             | [Choose a Pod](https://docs.runpod.io/pods/choose-a-pod)                             |
| An interactive machine for notebooks, SSH, or an IDE.           | A Pod.                                                                                              | [Connect to a Pod](https://docs.runpod.io/pods/connect-to-a-pod)                     |
| An always-on service with a stable address.                     | A Pod.                                                                                              | [Expose ports](https://docs.runpod.io/pods/configuration/expose-ports)               |
| Multi-node training or HPC.                                     | [Instant Clusters](https://docs.runpod.io/instant-clusters).                                        | [Slurm clusters](https://docs.runpod.io/instant-clusters/slurm-clusters)             |

## How a migration goes

Every guide follows the same eight steps, so you can run them in order or jump to the one you need.

1. List what runs on the other platform and find the code that calls it. Consoles often hold resources that no file in your repo mentions.
2. Create an account, get an [API key](https://docs.runpod.io/get-started/credentials), and install the tools you'll use: [runpodctl](https://docs.runpod.io/runpodctl/overview), the [Runpod SDK](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/overview), the [MCP server](https://docs.runpod.io/get-started/mcp-servers), or [Terraform](https://docs.runpod.io/integrations/terraform/overview).
3. Use the table above, then pick a GPU that fits the model. GPU stock varies by data center, so check what's available before you commit to a type.
4. Most container images run on Runpod unchanged if they're built for `linux/amd64`. Platform-specific contracts, such as a handler signature or a health route, need a small port.
5. Copy datasets and checkpoints to a [network volume](https://docs.runpod.io/storage/network-volumes). For models on Hugging Face, [cached models](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/endpoints/model-caching) skip the copy.
6. Create the Pod or endpoint from the console, runpodctl, the REST API, the SDK, or Terraform.
7. Change the URL, the auth header, and the request shape in the code that calls the workload. Put the new values behind configuration so you can switch back.
8. Send real requests to both deployments and compare. Shift traffic, then stop what's still billing on the other platform.

## Migrate with a coding agent

The Runpod plugin for coding agents includes a migration skill, `runpod-cloud-migrate`. It scans your repository for the platforms it depends on, opens the matching playbook, and proposes a plan before it changes anything. It migrates one workload at a time and verifies each with a real request.

1. The plugin installs the skills and connects the hosted MCP server:

   ```bash
   claude plugin marketplace add runpod/runpod-plugins-official
   claude plugin install runpod@runpod
   ```

   Install the skills for your agent, then connect the hosted MCP server:

   ```bash
   npx skills add runpod/runpod-plugins-official --skill '*' --agent AGENT_ID --global
   npx @runpod/mcp-server@latest add --client CLIENT_ID
   ```

   Replace `AGENT_ID` and `CLIENT_ID` with your agent's ID, for example `cursor` or `codex`.

   The MCP server signs you in with your Runpod account, so you don't need an API key to start. See [Agent skills](https://docs.runpod.io/get-started/agent-skills) and [MCP servers](https://docs.runpod.io/get-started/mcp-servers) for details.
2. Open your project and paste this prompt. In Claude Code, you can run `/runpod:migrate-cloud` instead.

   ```text
   Use the runpod-cloud-migrate skill to move this project to Runpod.

   1. Inventory the repository first and show me which platforms it uses and where.
   2. For each workload, propose where it lands on Runpod, what changes in the code,
      what data has to move, and anything that has no direct equivalent.
   3. Show me the plan and an hourly cost estimate. Wait for my approval before you
      create anything on Runpod.
   4. Migrate one workload at a time, starting with the smallest. Verify each one with
      a real request and show me the result.
   5. Keep the current deployment callable behind a config switch so I can roll back.
   6. Don't stop, change, or delete anything on the platform we're leaving unless I
      name the resource and approve it.
   ```
3. The agent stops after the inventory and plan. Check the targets, the GPU choice, and the list of gaps, then approve it. Nothing billable is created before that point.

## Get help

If a guide is wrong or a step fails, [open an issue on GitHub](https://github.com/runpod/docs/issues). For large or committed workloads, [talk to the Runpod sales team](https://ecykq.share.hsforms.com/2MZdZATC3Rb62Dgci7knjbA) about capacity planning and pricing.

# Migrate from Vast.ai to Runpod

Move Vast.ai instances, templates, volumes, Serverless endpoints, and automation code to Runpod Pods, Serverless, and REST API v2.

This guide is for teams that run GPU workloads on [Vast.ai](https://vast.ai) and want to run them on Runpod. Vast [instances](https://docs.vast.ai/guides/instances/overview) (on-demand, interruptible, and reserved) map to Runpod [Pods](https://docs.runpod.io/pods/overview), [Vast Serverless](https://docs.vast.ai/guides/serverless/index) endpoints, workergroups, and PyWorkers map to Runpod [Serverless](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/overview) endpoints, workers, and handlers, and Vast's machine-local [volumes](https://docs.vast.ai/guides/instances/storage/volumes) map to network volumes and global volumes. When you finish, your images, data, deploy scripts, and client code run against Runpod, and nothing is still billing on Vast.

> **Tip**
>
> You can hand most of this migration to a coding agent. See [Migrate with a coding agent](#migrate-with-a-coding-agent).

## How Vast.ai maps to Runpod

The biggest structural change is how you get a GPU. On Vast you search a marketplace of offers from individual hosts and rent one specific machine. On Runpod you name a GPU type (and optionally a data center), and the scheduler places your container.

| Vast.ai concept                                                     | Runpod equivalent                                                                                                                                                                                          | Notes                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Instance (Docker container on a rented offer)                       | [Pod](https://docs.runpod.io/pods/overview)                                                                                                                                                                | Both are containers with dedicated GPUs. A Pod is created from a GPU type ID, not an offer ID.                                                   |
| Offer search (`vastai search offers`)                               | GPU catalog: `runpodctl gpu list`, `runpodctl datacenter list`, `GET /v2/catalog/gpus`                                                                                                                     | The catalog reports stock per GPU type and data center. There's no per-machine reliability score, bandwidth price, or host choice.               |
| On-demand instance                                                  | On-demand Pod                                                                                                                                                                                              | Resources are dedicated to your Pod and can't be displaced by other users.                                                                       |
| Interruptible instance (`--bid_price`)                              | On-demand Pod                                                                                                                                                                                              | `runpodctl`, REST API v2, and the Terraform provider create on-demand Pods. See [What has no direct equivalent](#what-has-no-direct-equivalent). |
| Reserved instance (`vastai prepay instance`)                        | On-demand Pod                                                                                                                                                                                              | Runpod has no self-serve prepay discount. See [What has no direct equivalent](#what-has-no-direct-equivalent).                                   |
| Verified machines, `datacenter=true`, Secure Cloud filter           | Secure Cloud (default) and Community Cloud                                                                                                                                                                 | Set with `--cloud-type` or REST `cloud`. Secure Cloud also accepts `--compliance` and `--country-code` filters.                                  |
| Virtual machine instance (`vms_enabled=true`)                       | No equivalent                                                                                                                                                                                              | Pods are containers. See [What has no direct equivalent](#what-has-no-direct-equivalent).                                                        |
| Launch modes: entrypoint, SSH, Jupyter                              | One Pod type, with `--ssh` and `startJupyter` as options                                                                                                                                                   | Enabling SSH on a Pod doesn't replace your image's entrypoint.                                                                                   |
| `--onstart-cmd`, `--args`, `--entrypoint`                           | Start command: `--docker-args`, REST `cmd` and `entrypoint`                                                                                                                                                | There's no separate on-start script.                                                                                                             |
| `--env '-e KEY=value'` (Docker options)                             | `--env '{"KEY":"value"}'`, REST `env`                                                                                                                                                                      | JSON object, not Docker flags.                                                                                                                   |
| `--env '-p 8000:8000'`                                              | `--ports "8000/http,22/tcp"`, REST `ports`                                                                                                                                                                 | Each port is HTTP (proxied) or TCP (public IP).                                                                                                  |
| UDP port mapping (`-p 8082:8082/udp`)                               | No equivalent                                                                                                                                                                                              | Pods don't support UDP.                                                                                                                          |
| Template (`--template_hash`)                                        | [Template](https://docs.runpod.io/pods/templates/overview) (`--template-id`)                                                                                                                               | Pod templates and Serverless templates are separate.                                                                                             |
| Container storage (`--disk`)                                        | Container disk plus volume disk                                                                                                                                                                            | Container disk is erased when a Pod stops. Volume disk at `/workspace` persists across stops.                                                    |
| Local volume (`vastai create volume`)                               | [Network volume](https://docs.runpod.io/storage/network-volumes)                                                                                                                                           | A network volume is independent of any machine but pinned to one data center.                                                                    |
| Object storage you manage (S3, R2, GCS) for cross-host data         | Network volume, [global volume](https://docs.runpod.io/storage/globalvolume/overview), or keep your object storage                                                                                         | A global volume mounts in any data center.                                                                                                       |
| Cloud Sync (`vastai cloud copy`)                                    | [Cloud Sync](https://docs.runpod.io/pods/storage/cloud-sync), or the [S3-compatible API](https://docs.runpod.io/storage/s3-api) on network volumes                                                         | Provider lists differ. See [Step 5](#step-5-move-your-data-and-models).                                                                          |
| `vastai copy`, `scp`                                                | `runpodctl send` and `receive`, the [S3-compatible API](https://docs.runpod.io/storage/s3-api) on network volumes, `scp`, `rsync`                                                                          | See [Step 5](#step-5-move-your-data-and-models).                                                                                                 |
| Serverless endpoint plus workergroup                                | [Serverless endpoint](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/overview)                                                                                                                                          | One resource holds the image, GPU pools, and scaling settings.                                                                                   |
| Serverless worker running a PyWorker                                | Worker running a [handler](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/workers/handler-functions), or your own HTTP server on a [load-balancing endpoint](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/load-balancing/overview) | No benchmark step and no workload calculator.                                                                                                    |
| Deployments (`vastai.Deployment`, `@app.remote`, beta)              | Runpod SDK app (`runpod.App`, `@app.queue`, `@app.task`, `@app.api`)                                                                                                                                       | Both define remote functions in one Python file.                                                                                                 |
| OpenAI proxy (`https://openai.vast.ai/ENDPOINT_NAME`)               | vLLM worker route (`https://api.runpod.ai/v2/ENDPOINT_ID/openai/v1`)                                                                                                                                       | Runpod's route needs the real model name in `model`.                                                                                             |
| Model Library and Template Library                                  | [Hub](https://docs.runpod.io/hub/overview) and [Public Endpoints](https://docs.runpod.io/public-endpoints/overview)                                                                                        | Public Endpoints are hosted models you call without deploying anything.                                                                          |
| Account environment variables (`vastai create env-var`)             | [Secrets](https://docs.runpod.io/pods/templates/secrets), referenced as `{{ RUNPOD_SECRET_name }}`                                                                                                         | Secrets are referenced per template or Pod, not injected into every container.                                                                   |
| Docker login (`--login '-u USER -p TOKEN REGISTRY'`)                | Registry credential (`runpodctl registry create`, `--registry-auth-id`)                                                                                                                                    | Stored once, referenced by ID.                                                                                                                   |
| Pricing: per-host rates, per second, separate storage and bandwidth | Listed rates per GPU type, per second, no ingress or egress fees                                                                                                                                           | See [Pod pricing](https://docs.runpod.io/pods/pricing) and [Serverless pricing](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/pricing).                      |
| Prepaid credits, autobilling                                        | Prepaid credits, auto-pay                                                                                                                                                                                  | See [Billing](https://docs.runpod.io/accounts-billing/billing).                                                                                  |
| Infrastructure as code: scripts over the `vastai` CLI or REST API   | [Terraform provider](https://docs.runpod.io/integrations/terraform/overview) `runpod/runpod`, built on REST API v2                                                                                         | You can keep scripting with `runpodctl` and REST instead.                                                                                        |
| `vastai` CLI                                                        | [`runpodctl`](https://docs.runpod.io/runpodctl/overview)                                                                                                                                                   | JSON output by default.                                                                                                                          |
| `vastai` Python package (`VastAI`, `Serverless`)                    | [Runpod SDK](https://docs.runpod.io/sdk/overview) (`pip install runpod`)                                                                                                                                   | Apps, an endpoint client, the worker SDK, and an API wrapper.                                                                                    |
| REST API (`https://console.vast.ai/api/v0`)                         | [REST API v2](https://docs.runpod.io/api-reference-v2/overview) (`https://api.runpod.io/v2`)                                                                                                               | Both use `Authorization: Bearer`.                                                                                                                |
| API key (`VAST_API_KEY`, `~/.config/vastai/vast_api_key`)           | API key (`RUNPOD_API_KEY`, `~/.runpod/config.toml`)                                                                                                                                                        | Both support scoped keys.                                                                                                                        |
| Teams and team roles                                                | [Organizations](https://docs.runpod.io/organizations/orgs-overview), roles, and groups                                                                                                                     |                                                                                                                                                  |
| `vastai logs`, `vastai get endpt-logs`                              | `runpodctl pod logs`, `GET /v2/pods/POD_ID/logs`, [Serverless logs](https://docs.runpod.io/serverless/development/logs)                                                                                    |                                                                                                                                                  |
| Agent skill and plugins (`vast-ai/vast-cli`)                        | [Agent skills](https://docs.runpod.io/get-started/agent-skills) and the [MCP server](https://docs.runpod.io/get-started/mcp-servers)                                                                       |                                                                                                                                                  |

## What's different

### What works differently

**You pick a GPU type, not a machine.** A Vast create call takes an offer ID from a search. A Runpod create call takes a GPU type ID such as `NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090` and places it. The create call doesn't search for capacity or fall back to another GPU, so automation that looped over offers becomes a loop over GPU types or data centers that you're willing to accept. Stock varies by data center and changes between a catalog read and a create.

**Your image's entrypoint keeps running.** Vast's SSH and Jupyter launch modes replace the image entrypoint and run your `--onstart-cmd` instead. Runpod has no launch modes. SSH is an option on the Pod (`--ssh`, on by default in `runpodctl`), and your image's `ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD` run as built unless you override them. Move the contents of an on-start script into the Pod's start command or into the image.

**Environment variables are visible in SSH sessions without extra steps.** On Vast you may have added `env >> /etc/environment` to on-start scripts so SSH and Jupyter sessions could see your variables. Drop that line. On Runpod you pass `env` as a JSON object, and the Pod's own variables use the `RUNPOD_` prefix.

**Ports are typed.** Vast maps each `-p` port to a random external port on the host's shared IP over plain TCP. On Runpod, a port declared as `PORT/http` is served at `https://POD_ID-PORT.proxy.runpod.net` over HTTPS, and a port declared as `PORT/tcp` gets a public IP and a mapped external port. The proxy URL is public and unauthenticated, and it closes connections that run longer than 100 seconds, so add authentication in your app and use a TCP port for long-lived connections. Declare every port you need: the console accepts up to 10 HTTP ports per Pod. Requesting a port above 70000 for a matching internal and external port works the same way on both platforms.

**Stopping a Pod clears its container disk.** A stopped Vast instance keeps everything on its disk. A stopped Pod keeps only the volume disk (mounted at `/workspace` by default) or an attached network volume. Anything written elsewhere in the container is gone after a stop, a restart caused by a config change, or a terminate. Write checkpoints and outputs under `/workspace`.

**Storage isn't tied to a machine.** A Vast volume can only attach to instances on the physical machine where it was created. A Runpod network volume attaches to any Pod or Serverless worker in its data center, and a global volume attaches in any data center. You size a network volume up front and can grow it later. You can also change a Pod's container disk and volume disk size with `runpodctl pod update`, where Vast fixes disk size at creation.

**Bandwidth isn't billed.** Vast hosts set per-GB upload and download prices. Runpod Pods bill compute and storage per second with no ingress or egress fees. Remove `inet_up_cost` and `inet_down_cost` terms from any cost model you carry over.

**Status fields have different names and one false friend.** Vast scripts decide from `actual_status`. Runpod's REST API returns one `status` field, and `runpodctl` adds `runtimeStatus`. On Vast, `exited` means the container crashed. On Runpod, `EXITED` means the Pod is stopped and can be started again, and `ERROR` is the failure state. See the [status map](#status-map).

**Serverless is one resource, and requests go through Runpod.** A Vast client asks the Serverless engine for a worker (`/route/`), then sends the request to that worker's address with signed `auth_data`. A Runpod client sends every request to a fixed endpoint URL with your API key, and Runpod queues or load-balances it. There's no workergroup: the endpoint itself holds the image, GPU pools, and scaling settings.

**Serverless scaling uses different inputs.** Vast scales on measured load against benchmarked worker performance (`min_load`, `target_util`, `cold_mult`, `cold_workers`). Runpod scales on queue delay or request count, between a minimum and maximum worker count, with an idle timeout. Endpoints scale to zero by default.

### What has no direct equivalent

On the Runpod side:

- **UDP ports.** Vast maps UDP ports (`-p 8082:8082/udp`, `VAST_UDP_PORT_X`). Pods don't support UDP. Move the protocol to TCP (for example WebRTC over TCP or TURN over TCP, or WireGuard replaced by a TCP-based tunnel), or keep the UDP-facing component elsewhere and connect it to the Pod over TCP.
- **Bidding for interruptible capacity.** Vast lets you set a bid and pauses the instance when you're outbid. Pod creation in `runpodctl` and REST API v2 has no bid or interruptible field. Run these jobs as on-demand Pods with checkpoints, as a Serverless queue endpoint that scales to zero between jobs, or as an `@app.task` function that provisions a Pod per call and terminates it when the function returns.
- **Self-serve reserved discounts.** `vastai prepay instance` has no counterpart. Runpod's savings plans are deprecated and can't be purchased. For committed capacity or custom pricing, [contact sales](https://www.runpod.io/contact).
- **Choosing a host.** Filters such as `reliability`, `inet_down`, `dlperf`, `static_ip`, and `machine_id` don't exist. You choose a GPU type, a cloud tier, a data center or country, a minimum CUDA version, and minimum vCPU and RAM per GPU.
- **Virtual machines and Docker inside the instance.** Vast VM instances support systemd and nested containers. Pods are containers and don't run Docker Compose. Package each service as its own image and run one Pod per service (NVIDIA GPU Pods in the same account can reach each other over [global networking](https://docs.runpod.io/pods/networking)), or run the services as processes in one image.
- **ARM hosts.** Vast lists `cpu_arch=arm64` offers. Runpod images must be `linux/amd64`.
